Opposite early and late program directions persisted after removing shared genes. No external program met the prespecified prospective criterion. These findings support stage- and compartment-dependent remodeling of EBV-associated B-cell transcription rather than persistence of a stable RNA signature. They distinguish cellular trafficking from transcriptional-state preservation and show that cross-system molecular resemblance alone cannot establish ancestry. EBV-directed biomarker studies should integrate host transcription with virologic, clonotypic, antigen-specific, epigenetic, and longitudinal evidence.
organization: University of Idaho; Wayne State University

title: AI agent startup LangChain hits $3B valuation
abstract: Agent management startup LangChain has raised a $300 million Series C at a $3 billion valuation led by CapitalG, with participation from investors, including Singapore’s GIC, DFJ Growth, IVP, and Sapphire Ventures, the company announced on Friday. That’s more than double its $1.25 billion valuation when it raised $125 million about a year ago , led by IVP. LangChain began in 2022 as a popular open source project that handled the kinds of tasks that early-stage LLMs found difficult, like searching the web, calling APIs, and interacting with databases. As the frontier AI labs delivered harnesses that now competently do those tasks, LangChain turned its focus toward managing AI agents. It has apparently found its stride in this highly competitive area with a simple message: letting businesses own their own intelligence. With its open source roots, the startup says its agent creation and management software, LangSmith, is not trying to lock users into any particular model, cloud, or ecosystem, unlike the major clouds or frontier AI labs. It also promises that LangSmith will contain agent behavior and is easy to use. True, there are plenty of other startups pitching similar advantages these days and also doing well ( case in point is newcomer Mintive ). However, LangChain has had a head start and now claims 7,000 LangSmith customers, including big-name startups like Harvey, Rippling, and Clay, and enterprises like Nvidia, Toyota, and Salesforce.

title: Export-banned Nvidia chips are behind China’s most powerful AI models — uh-oh, Jensen!
abstract: The leading open-weight models developed by Chinese companies were trained on Nvidia chips that the U.S. government restricted from shipping to its largest geopolitical rival, a new research effort claims. The apparently widespread access to Blackwell GPUs among Chinese frontier labs shows the magnitude of the problem facing the leading chip designer. Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang left the company this week after admitting to his affair with Alice Huang, executive of Megaspeed, a company implicated in smuggling Nvidia chips into China. Alice Huang has also been alleged to be an agent of China’s intelligence service. While Jensen Huang’s relationships with a customer and two employees have drawn the most public interest, Nvidia’s potential corporate liability for export control violations likely factored into its decision to part ways with Huang. U.S. export controls are intended to protect the country’s leadership in AI capabilities against China, but Huang has long sought to open up that market. Blackwell GPUs are banned from export to China or Chinese-owned firms, while the Trump administration allows Nvidia to export the H200, a less powerful chip, provided shipments take a circuitous shipping route that allows the U.S. to claim a 25% tariff. Will DePue, a former OpenAI researcher who leads the nonprofit research group Unemployment Labs, analyzed the weights — the unique structure — of large language models released openly by DeepSeek, Moonshot AI, MiniMax, and Ant Group. The weights still reflect the configurations of the chips used to train them, and DePue was able to find compelling evidence that the most closely watched models, including Moonshot’s Kimi’s K3 releases and DeepSeek’s V4 models, bear fingerprints from training on Blackwell chips. White House technology adviser Michael Kratsios said earlier this year that Moonshot had used export-banned Nvidia chips, citing U.S. intelligence sources. Epoch AI, a nonprofit research organization, estimates that about two million advanced chips entered China in 2024 and 2025 through schemes designed to hide their final destination. That doesn’t mean that these models were trained entirely on Nvidia chips, or that export control laws were necessarily violated; the chips could have been in an offshore data center, which has proven a popular way for Chinese firms to access compute and driven an industrial revolution in Malaysia. Epoch’s data estimates that 275,000 Nvidia AI accelerators were imported to Malaysia in 2024 and 2025. However, the ostensible goal of the export bans is to prevent exactly that: Chinese AI labs training on the most powerful chips. China hawks have long called for stronger controls on who uses chips, not just who owns them or where they are installed. “If we care about the U.S. tech edge, it doesn’t make any sense to me that you would not allow Chinese companies to access chips in mainland China or Hong Kong and Macau, but then say, actually, if you just go over to Malaysia, you can do whatever you want,” Sam Bresnick, a researcher at the Georgetown Center for Security and Emerging Technology, told TechCrunch this summer. Megaspeed, the company led by Alice Huang, has been at the center of that trade for several years through its subsidiary Speedmatrix, and has been the subject of investigations by both the U.S. and S i ngaporean government. Friday, Bloomberg also reported that a company with links to Alice Huang was involved in smuggling banned Nvidia chips to a data center in Shanghai. In May, the short-selling research firm Culper published a report arguing that Nvidia had a “ China problem ” because a significant share of its revenue was driven by Chinese demand, either through remote data centers or smuggling in violation of U.S. law. It detailed Megaspeed’s relationship with Nvidia and alleged that Alice Huang’s companies are backed by Chinese firms that are barred from accessing U.S. chips. Ironically, short-seller Culper’s bet against Nvidia wasn’t driven by the expectation of a U.S. government crackdown. Instead, it was focused on the Chinese government’s response to the bans, which was to recommit to its domestic chip industry. If China succeeds, billions of dollars in Chinese demand for Nvidia chips could dry up. Some 600,000 H200 chips are reportedly stockpiled in Hong Kong, awaiting shipment into China. While Chinese companies might want the chips, observers have no consensus on why they haven’t been cleared for import. Graham Webster, a research scholar at Stanford who focuses on U.S.-China technology policy, said he doesn’t buy the idea that holding the chips back would drive domestic production, since demand for chips is so large. Other theories for the hold-up include preparation for a potential trade deal that would involve importing a large volume of U.S. goods, or concerns about potential surveillance technology in the chips. For now, U.S. companies have limited obligations to track what their customers do with controlled goods like AI chips. However, Jensen Huang’s personal and professional entanglements with Alice Huang create a much bigger problem for Nvidia if government investigators confirm that chip smuggling took place and that he was aware of it. Nvidia and Huang have both vouched for Megaspeed’s data centers, saying Nvidia officials had visited them to confirm they were legitimate. The U.S. government’s treatment of Nvidia and Megaspeed is also under scrutiny. Secretary of Commerce Howard Lutnick, who oversees the agencies that license chip exports, could reportedly lose his job after reports that his investigators failed to uncover suspicious chip buyers and were too cozy with Nvidia officials.

title: ChatGPT’s new Wallet lets AI agents shop and check out for you
abstract: ChatGPT can now shop for you. On Friday, OpenAI launched a new wallet feature that lets its agents, called dots , help you decide what to buy and then complete the purchase on your behalf. The option will initially be available to a limited number of U.S. ChatGPT Pro subscribers, ages 18 and up, with a U.S.-issued Visa, Mastercard, or American Express. OpenAI says that users are fully in control of the purchases, as they’re able to review the items, the total, and the payment card that will be used to complete the transaction before the checkout occurs. In addition, users will approve the purchases directly with a security check like Face ID or a fingerprint, which creates a record of their transaction. The addition comes as consumer-facing AI tools are working to find the right product-market fit, in terms of how they can help people be more efficient as they complete various tasks. While companies like DoorDash and Uber have so far reported low numbers of orders placed by AI agents, Meta’s Muse, which now has over 10 million users, has seen AI-assisted shopping become a top activity on its app. Other personal AI agents, like Instinct, also support making purchases on users’ behalf. It’s no surprise, then, that OpenAI would want to enter this space more with an agentic shopping feature of its own. To get started, ChatGPT subscribers add their eligible payment cards to the new ChatGPT Wallet, then ask their dot to help with a purchase. (This setup is a one-time thing; users don’t have to re-enter their payment information every time they buy.) When it’s time to transact, ChatGPT’s Wallet charges the selected card using a payment token, which is a substitute for the user’s actual card details, so that information isn’t shared with either the dot or the merchant. The merchant will automatically receive what it needs to fulfill the order from the dot, like the shipping address and contact information, OpenAI says. The company notes that customers who shop via their dots will still be able to earn their credit card rewards and be able to take advantage of protections that typically come with cards, like being able to dispute transactions. The limited availability at launch will allow OpenAI to test and improve the feature and its capabilities before rolling it out more broadly. In the future, the company plans to offer users more control over the feature by allowing them to set spending limits or configure other parameters around purchase categories or time periods, so they can pre-approve purchases that their agent can then handle more autonomously. It also aims to make the agentic shopping feature an option at a broader number of supported retailers. This could be a challenge in some areas, where retailers are blocking AI agents from using their site ; on the shopping front, the largest retailer to ban AI agents is Amazon, as it aims to steer users to its own AI agent, Alexa, instead. To help retailers adapt to agentic commerce, OpenAI also published a Commerce Partner Playbook that offers tools and guidance to sites that want to support customers using agents.

title: The unfolding Jensen Huang scandal: a timeline
abstract: Nvidia co-founder and now former CEO Jensen Huang has never been as prone to controversy as AI leaders like OpenAI’s Sam Altman or SpaceXAI’s Elon Musk. But the 63-year-old industry kingpin recently admitted that he cheated on his wife of 40 years in affairs that could have ramifications beyond Huang’s personal life and U.S. national security. U.S. officials believe that one of Huang’s likely romantic interests, Megaspeed executive Alice Huang, is a Chinese spy who has been feeding information back to Beijing. (Alice Huang, a Chinese citizen, is of no relation to Jensen Huang.) Megaspeed is a Singapore-based AI infrastructure company that reportedly purchased $4.8 billion worth of Nvidia chips over the last two years. The U.S. and Singapore have both previously investigated Megaspeed over suspicions that the firm was illegally sharing chips with China. The Justice Department has since taken over the federal investigation into the company, The New York Times has reported. The story took a sudden turn on Wednesday. Citing five people who worked at Nvidia, the Times reported that Huang also had an extramarital relationship with Kimberly Powell, the company’s vice president of healthcare, who reports directly to him. Nvidia, Huang and Powell have not confirmed the report. Reached by a Times reporter, Huang reportedly said, “I don’t think you should be talking to me directly,” before hanging up. By early Thursday morning, Huang was no longer CEO of the company he co-founded 33 years ago. Then, Thursday afternoon, Reuters dropped another bombshell, publishing a report alleging that Huang had yet another extramarital affair with another unnamed Nvidia employee. The U.S. and China are embroiled in a fierce technological arms race to build the most advanced AI infrastructure, which could shape each country’s economic future, military prowess, and capacity for innovation. Nvidia is valuable in this competition as one of the world’s largest makers of AI chips, which are essential for accelerating AI development. But as an American company, Nvidia faces government restrictions on the sale of its most powerful chips to Chinese entities. As the controversy unfolds, we are organizing the most relevant events into a reverse-chronological timeline to keep you up to date. November 13, 2026: Huang was not confident in his successor, Colette Kress; reports describe Huang as ‘broken’ More reports continue to roll out that illustrate the shock and severity of Huang’s resignation from Nvidia. Bloomberg reported that Huang looked “broken and shattered, his legendary energy depleted” by the time he surrendered his role on Wednesday night, uttering phrases like “whatever” and “I don’t care.” Separately, The Wall Street Journal reported that Huang had been critical of his CFO and current interim CEO, Colette Kress. Huang is said to have described Kress as “a deer in the headlights” during a presentation this summer, and he had described Kress as someone who could not help him steer strategy or decision-making. November 12, 2026: Democrats launch investigation into Nvidia; Huang and Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick summoned to testify before Senate Banking Committee In a scathing letter sent to Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick, Representative Richard Neal (D-MA) and Senator Ron Wyden (D-OR) said they will investigate how the Trump administration handled Nvidia’s chip sales to China, especially after Trump was briefed about Huang’s relationship with a purported Chinese spy. “Although [Lutnick] and President Trump were reportedly briefed on this intelligence, the Administration did not appear to acknowledge this evident national security threat. On the contrary: despite reportedly learning of Mr. Huang’s compromising relationship last fall, President Trump granted Nvidia permission to sell its advanced H200 AI chips to China in December 2025 in exchange for a cut of the export sales,” the letter states. That same evening, Senator Tim Scott (R-SC) requested that Huang and Lutnick both testify before the Senate Banking Committee. “The American people deserve answers,” Scott wrote on X. November 12, 2026: Huang was having a third affair with another Nvidia employee, according to Reuters After Huang was already ousted from Nvidia, we continued to learn more incriminating claims about the former CEO. According to Reuters, Huang had a third affair with an additional, unnamed employee of Nvidia. November 12, 2026: Jensen Huang resigns, CFO Colette Kress named as interim CEO; Huang agrees to testify before Congress Nvidia said its board had accepted Huang’s resignation on Wednesday. The company’s current CFO, Colette Kress , will take over as interim CEO while still fulfilling her CFO duties. Nvidia is expected to conduct a larger search to determine a permanent successor to Huang. Harvey C. Jones, a managing partner of Square Wave Ventures and former CEO of Synopsys, was appointed as the company’s first-ever chair of the board of directors. Jones has been on Nvidia’s board since 1993. Later in the day, Huang confirmed that he would testify in Congress at some point before Thanksgiving, which falls on November 26. “Jensen and I have been very at odds as some of you already know on export controls, but Nvidia is a very important company to the United States of America,” House Foreign Affairs Committee Chairman Brian Mast said to reporters. “I don’t want to see anything hurt in Nvidia, but he has some very serious questions to answer.” The testimony is expected to take place behind closed doors, but Mast believes the briefing will be recorded and transcribed. November 11, 2026: Nvidia’s stock drops as board reportedly preps to oust CEO Jensen Huang After reports of a second extramarital affair, Nvidia’s board reportedly plans to meet to discuss Huang’s future at the company, per The Wall Street Journal. Stock fell about 8% in after-hours trading on Wednesday and is down 11% in the past five days. Huang famously delegates very little and has about 60 direct reports, he has said . The company has not had an obvious successor or a succession plan. November 11, 2026: Huang also had an affair with an Nvidia executive who reports to him, NYT says The New York Times reported that Jensen Huang also had an affair with Nvidia vice president of healthcare Kimberly Powell, who reports directly to the CEO. According to the report, Huang and Powell were captured on film “being affectionate” at a hotel during a conference earlier this year. November 11, 2026: Congress plans to subpoena Huang to answer questions about affair Huang has not responded to a request from three Republican congressmen to appear for a closed-door briefing for questioning about his affair with an alleged Chinese spy. House China Committee Chairman John Moolenaar said Wednesday on Fox Business that if Huang doesn’t agree to the briefing, he’ll likely be subpoenaed . November 9, 2026: Huang pulls out of various speaking engagements The Nvidia CEO pulled out of upcoming speaking engagements at the ElevenLabs Summit and Anthropic CEO Forum. November 9-10, 2026: Details emerge about the business relationships between Nvidia and the alleged spy Alice Huang and her family reportedly built a network of companies in China and Singapore to acquire Nvidia chips, including founding a Chinese company called Shanghai Century Litong. Founded in 2023, it became an Nvidia-preferred cloud partner, giving it priority access to chips, The Information reported . The Information also reported that Shanghai Century Litong facilitated buying $7.5 billion worth of Nvidia’s chips, including banned chips. Nvidia’s head lawyer, Tim Teter, intervened in a 2025 U.S. government probe surrounding the suspected smuggling of AI chips by Megaspeed International, Bloomberg reported . Teter contacted Commerce Under Secretary Jeffrey Kessler asking questions about whether the Trump administration played a role in detaining Alice Huang.

title: ElevenLabs’ new app combines meeting note-taking and dictation for teams
abstract: In the last few months, Fireflies , Wispr Flow , and Granola have all released competing capabilities in the dictation and meeting note-taking space. The newest entrant in that category is voice AI giant ElevenLabs , which this week released an experimental app called ElevenAI that combines meeting note-taking, dictation, and agent integration. Launched during its 11/11 Summit in New York, ElevenAI is still in preview, and you have to sign up for early access instead of just downloading an app. ElevenLabs, valued at $22 billion , is very much positioning this as a product that lives within a team as compared to a productivity tool for an individual. ElevenAI packs all the features typically found in other apps in the category. It can take meeting notes across your meetings and notify other participants that the conversation is being recorded. Users can query data across meetings and get live assistance during a chat, helping them recall a key detail from older conversations. ElevenLabs also allows companies to integrate ElevenAgent and take follow-up actions such as writing a draft email based on meeting notes. Plus, there’s a dictation feature, which lets users convert speech to cleaned-up text in any app with support for over 90 languages. The company said that the app is capable of understanding industry-specific terms across dictation and meeting transcription. ElevenAI allows the company to use its own model as a showcase and also utilize its agent platforms for better context funneling. The startup’s positioning might not be to directly compete in the productivity market, but rather to give enterprise teams an option to not buy licenses to a notetaker and use its solution instead. All meeting-related tools are rushing to become central knowledge hubs for companies while aiming to automate knowledge extraction and follow-up actions In the last week, the company also launched its v3 series of Scribe speech-to-text models with live transcription capabilities and the ability for companies to fine-tune models using their own data, a tool to pick the right language model based on use case , and a routine creator that automates tasks based on the transcript.

title: Israel’s VCs see opportunity for challengers in Nvidia’s turmoil
abstract: Former Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang’s resignation has been received with worry in Israel, the company’s “second home,” as Huang described it in 2023. The company’s importance flows both ways, as the semiconductor giant has provided a major boost to Israel’s economic forecasts in recent years. Intel, Microsoft, and many homegrown startups also conduct a sizable share of their R&D in Israel. But owing to Nvidia’s stronghold on AI given the centrality of its GPUs for training LLMs and using them, many in the country are wondering how much of a reshuffle will result from the company’s leadership crisis. As with everything at Nvidia, Huang drove the company to acquire Israeli chipmaker Mellanox for $6.9 billion in 2019 and use the company as the base for its largest R&D facility outside of the U.S. Nvidia also made plans to build a multibillion-dollar campus in northern Israel. “Jensen brought Nvidia to Israel with the acquisition of Mellanox, so there is a strong positive sentiment towards Nvidia and Jensen in Israel’s tech community,” Israeli repeat cybersecurity entrepreneur Pavel Gurvich told TechCrunch. Beyond the 6,000 locals Nvidia employs, the bigger question is whether the company will remain as committed to Israel with someone else at the helm. As a result, his line of succession is being observed just as closely by those who hope the company continues to do so as by those who don’t want it to happen. The latter have already gathered that they may be in for disappointment. In a 2023 interview that is now doing the rounds on X, interim CEO Colette Kress had declared that as Nvidia’s CFO, she typically started her day “with Israel meetings, and only then continue[d] to California.” Kress may not remain in charge in the long run, but the many names floated for the role include two Israelis , Apple’s Johny Srouji and Nvidia’s Michael Kagan — although they’re not at the top of the still quite tentative list . Regardless of who gets chosen, Huang’s successor will likely have less of a grip on Nvidia and the tech industry as a whole. But investors don’t think that would cause demand for Nvidia’s product to fade away. According to Yanai Oron, a general partner at Vertex Ventures Israel, “slower decisions at Nvidia could give competitors an opening, but if that uncertainty also slows AI spending, they could end up with a bigger share of a smaller opportunity.” Nvidia has been responsible for a vast share of the spending in the global AI industry. Under Huang’s leadership, the company used its cash reserves to massively invest across the spectrum, both in companies and in its own next-generation chips . Such an empire may not be doomed to fall with its architect’s ouster, but it does seem less likely to become a full-on monopoly. According to Adi Levanon, a founder and managing partner at Selah Ventures, “[Huang’s] departure doesn’t dismantle Nvidia’s technology or ecosystem, but it could give competitors more room to shape what comes next.” And now that companies globally are deploying increasingly demanding AI agents into their workflows, there’s been a lot of interest — and some venture capital — flowing into developers of AI-specific chips and inference software that could compete with Nvidia’s. “These challengers now have a window to prove a different approach delivers better economics; a leadership change alone won’t win them the business,” Levanon said.

title: Jensen Huang didn’t show confidence in his successor, report says
abstract: Former Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang described Colette Kress, the company’s CFO who has now replaced him as interim CEO, as “a deer in the headlights” during a presentation earlier in the summer, the Wall Street Journal reported , citing an anonymous source. Huang made the comment during a meeting with Nvidia’s finance team about the company’s plans to provide guarantees worth billions of dollars to data center operators that couldn’t afford to buy its chips up front, according to the report. He reportedly also said Kress was a person who couldn’t help him steer strategy or decision-making. Kress has been with Nvidia for over 13 years now , after serving as SVP and CFO of Cisco’s Business Technology and Operations Finance. The report said she has questioned Nvidia’s program-focused, credit-based deals involving Huang’s son-in-law Nico Caprez, and wanted to know how to decide which deals are beneficial, how to value guarantees, and determine returns. Earlier in the year, she had scaled back on Nvidia’s commitment for OpenAI’s ambitious Ohio data center project. The company was in talks to provide $250 billion in credit to OpenAI but ended up committing $105 billion . Huang resigned Thursday after reports of two extramarital affairs , including one with the company’s VP for healthcare, Kimberly Powell. The company is also investigating a possible Chinese espionage plot . After Huang’s resignation, Reuters reported that he was having a third affair with another employee . Nvidia is currently searching for a permanent CEO to replace Huang, who had the top job for over 33 years.

title: ChatGPT Wallet lets OpenAI’s Dots agents make purchases for you
abstract: AI News Tech ChatGPT Wallet lets OpenAI’s Dots agents make purchases for you OpenAI says ChatGPT Wallet won’t share your actual credit card info with its AI agents.﻿ OpenAI says ChatGPT Wallet won’t share your actual credit card info with its AI agents.﻿ by Stevie Bonifield Nov 13, 2026, 8:45 PM UTC Image: Cath Virginia / The Verge, Getty Images Stevie Bonifield is a news writer covering all things consumer tech. Stevie started out at Laptop Mag writing news and reviews on hardware, gaming, and AI. After launching its Dots AI agents platform earlier this year, OpenAI is launching a wallet for the agents. ChatGPT Wallet is rolling out starting today for ChatGPT Pro subscribers in the US aged 18 and older using a US billing address and “eligible US-issued American Express, Chase, Mastercard and Visa cards.” After adding a card to the wallet, your Dots agents can use it to buy things in response to your prompts, but they’ll check in with you each time before checking out. OpenAI’s support page says every purchase with ChatGPT Wallet requires a security check with biometric verification like Face ID or a fingerprint scan. Users have to approve every purchase from ChatGPT Wallet. Image: OpenAI After you review the AI agent’s purchase and sign off on it, OpenAI says that, similar to using tap to pay , Apple Pay , or Google Wallet , it substitutes your credit card details with a payment token, so your actual card info isn’t shared with your Dots agent or the business you’re buying from. Eventually, OpenAI says it expects “users to be able to delegate purchases entirely to their agent by setting clear parameters—such as spending limits, purchase categories, or time periods—and pre-approve those purchases.” ChatGPT Wallet might not work everywhere. Some retailers have restrictions on AI agents or block them altogether. Earlier this year, Amazon blocked Meta’s Muse agents. OpenAI says that in order for agents to use ChatGPT Wallet, “websites need to ensure agents are not inadvertently blocked, and payment and risk systems need to recognize legitimate purchases made by agents.” Follow topics and authors from this story to see more like this in your personalized homepage feed and to receive email updates. Stevie Bonifield AI News OpenAI Tech

title: What’s really at stake in the Jensen Huang saga
abstract: Vergecast Podcasts AI Policy What’s really at stake in the Jensen Huang saga On The Vergecast: The many spiraling stories in the AI world, the fate of streaming services, Mark Zuckerberg’s meat, and more. On The Vergecast: The many spiraling stories in the AI world, the fate of streaming services, Mark Zuckerberg’s meat, and more. by David Pierce Nov 13, 2026, 2:47 PM UTC David Pierce is editor-at-large and Vergecast co-host with over a decade of experience covering consumer tech. Previously, at Protocol, The Wall Street Journal, and Wired. One part of the saga surrounding Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang ended on Thursday, when Huang resigned from his position at the top of AI’s most important company. But in the coming weeks and months, a much bigger story may be about to unfold. A story about Nvidia’s dealings in China, about the US government’s willingness to turn a lot of blind eyes to protect a powerful ally, and about the very stability of the AI industry as a whole. It’s a lot. On this episode of The Vergecast , David and Nilay start by trying to unpack the many parts of the story. We’re all going to learn a lot more about Megaspeed than we ever planned or wanted, and we’re going to hear a lot of people — particularly newly elected Democrats — asking questions about who knew what and when. In the meantime, who will replace Huang as the AI industry’s front man? And will everyone survive the scrutiny that’s coming? After that, the hosts tackle a week filled with small-ish news from streaming services that adds up to Hollywood’s plan to properly take on TikTok . We’re about to find out whether microdramas, free tiers, and a deep obsession with vertical video will save the Netflixes and Paramounts of the world. Will it work? Probably not. Is it the only rational thing to try? You bet. Finally, in the lightning round, it’s time for Brendan Carr Is a Dummy, Mark Zuckerberg’s AI experiments , the Cybertruck era , and more. title: Claude’s Duet agent is a little neurotic and surprisingly helpful
abstract: AI Tech Reviews Claude’s Duet agent is a little neurotic and surprisingly helpful Duet is a decent helper, if a little jumpy at times. by Allison Johnson Nov 13, 2026, 2:00 PM UTC Let’s get to work. | Photo: Allison Johnson / The Verge Allison Johnson is a senior reviewer with over a decade of experience writing about consumer tech. She has a special interest in mobile photography and telecom. Previously, she worked at DPReview. Normally, the products I test don’t offer to help me write up my experience with them. Duet is different. Claude Duet is Anthropic’s AI agent for consumers, the latest attempt by an AI company to try to convince us that agents can be useful for people who don’t write code. It’s been an interesting couple of months: Instinct gave us an impressive text-based assistant , Meta offered us its cute little guy, Muse, to help us buy things , and OpenAI gave us the more work-oriented Dots . Claude Duet is even more focused on work than those. It’s also more consumer-friendly than Claude Cowork , which was more consumer-friendly than Claude Code — the coding agent that kicked off a whole hype cycle earlier this year. I’ve been testing it over the past week as I navigate a busy travel and work schedule. At turns it has been truly useful, kind of a nag, and very eager to write about itself. Duet is still a “research preview” according to Anthropic, and access is limited to Pro, Max, and Ultra subscribers in the US, with a waitlist to join. It’s not here to order you burritos, either; it’s for “professionals and small business owners” and is meant to use its judgment about what needs your attention most. Like Meta’s Muse, Duet has its own app. (If you’re keeping score at home, yes, it has been updated to fully support the iPhone Duo). Duet uses Claude’s characteristically cheery, minimalist design. The app is consumer-friendly and approachable. Once you’ve connected all the productivity and chat services you want, it’ll look for ways to help out with and suggest them as cards you can swipe left or right to hide or accept — kind of a to-do list Tinder. In the name of testing, I went all in on Duet and gave it everything: my work email, calendar, Google Docs, and Slack. This gave it plenty of grist for the mill in more ways than I’d even realized at first. Because our biweekly staff meeting is automatically summarized in an email from Gemini, and Duet had access to my email, it was able to connect the dots between something said in a meeting and a direct message in Slack. Duet also worked out who my boss is because we have a shared Google Doc for our weekly 1:1 meetings. AI is at its most useful when it can suck up lots of data, and Duet wasted no time doing so. Previous Next 1 / 2 You can swipe left or right on these cards to dismiss or get Duet started on them. Duet has started each morning by greeting me with a brief message and some quick highlights for my day, like reminding me to pack an item required for a video shoot before my flight. Below that, it would suggest to-dos, usually ending in an offer to help draft a message or add an item to an agenda. This has often been helpful, though it sometimes felt like interacting with a slightly neurotic personal assistant. In one instance, I’d emailed someone I interviewed for a story that the article was likely to go up on Tuesday and that I’d send a link when it did. I submitted my draft to my editors late at night on Monday, and Tuesday morning Duet was beside itself. It wasn’t quite 9AM yet when it pointed out that the story was still waiting for an edit and I needed to get on that — or else I wouldn’t be able to send the link I promised. The concern was a bit misplaced. And it didn’t pick up on the nuance in my message implying that this was not a hard deadline, nor the fact that it was only 7AM local time for my editor. This sometimes felt like interacting with a slightly neurotic personal assistant In other cases, it was surprisingly helpful. In planning out the next few weeks I’d missed the fact that upcoming time off would only leave me with a couple of working days before another big draft was due. Duet proposed a solution, offered to update the Google Doc with weekly notes for my editor, and drafted a Slack message for him noting the update. Reader, the message was a little too good. It copied my millennial habit of writing in all lowercase — which it pointed out in a slightly self-congratulatory aside — and used an abbreviation we often use to refer to our CMS. But it also shortened the word “signature” to “sig,” which I never would and made me laugh out loud. In any case, there’s no fooling anyone; the Slack message was tagged with a “sent with Claude” label. Duet often volunteered to help start my drafts, which is always a hard no for me. I’ll type up my own little blogs, thank you very much Claude. If you’re not a writer, I can see how taking care of little writing chores here and there would be helpful. But this started feeling like a Spider-Man-pointing-at-Spider-Man moment when the task it wanted to help with was reviewing itself. Maybe that’s how CEOs live It was a little uncanny, too. Even setting aside the fact that I was writing about Duet, it’s kind of weird knowing that it can read every email, draft, and Slack I send. It can read all of that because I opted in to sharing that data , and I knew full well what I was doing. But it’s another thing to see it in practice. I wonder if it would change how I work if I knew I didn’t really need to take responsibility for putting things on my calendar, writing down a to-do list, or paying attention in a meeting because Duet will just handle it. Maybe that’s how CEOs live. Not that I cherish creating calendar entries, but I wonder if I would end up feeling a bit disconnected from my workplace. I don’t think Duet or any other AI agent is quite ready to make us feel like we’re all the CEOs of our own little worlds. There’s a key word in the title “personal assistant”: personal. A person can pick up on nuances in tone to understand what’s a big deal and what isn’t. A person will pick up on communication norms and deploy them sensibly. A person can be tactful. Anthropic’s blog post mentions that the company is continuing to “test its judgment about when to message you,” so it’s possible Duet will calibrate a little better over time. But AI overall isn’t good at understanding nuance or tone, and it’s not clear if it ever will be. For me, Duet made it a little more clear what I want AI to do for me and what I don’t. Communication happens all over the place in a modern workplace — in emails, DMs, meetings, shared docs. Having AI find discrepancies that have been overlooked between all of these sources and point them out proactively is really helpful. I like it as a backstop for my own organizational systems, not as a replacement for them. I don’t like it in the creative process. Like, at all. I want to find “my own ways into and around a topic,” as Hank Green said of his own reliance on AI . If you send a robot to do the legwork, you miss the opportunity to stumble across something unexpected. It’s part of what makes the work enjoyable. And I’m certainly not about to let an agent review itself for me. You hear that, Duet? title: Build a Robot Pick-and-Place Simulation with SimReady Assets
abstract:
Back to Articles Build a Robot Pick-and-Place Simulation with SimReady Assets Enterprise + Article Published November 13, 2026 Upvote 5 Dillon Bailey dillonb-nv Follow nvidia Pomi Lee pomilee Follow nvidia Rishabh Chadha rchadha-nv Follow nvidia This walkthrough showcases a beverage can pick-and-place task that uses the UR17G arm , Robotiq 2F-140 gripper , and beverage can to compose a scene in Isaac Sim, check their behavior, and run a pick-and-place example with agent-generated controls. For robotics workflows, SimReady means an OpenUSD asset has been prepared with the properties needed for a defined simulation use case, such as collisions, mass, joints, and joint drives. SimReady Central , an open asset library on Hugging Face, lets you reuse robot and object assets with authored simulation properties and profile-validation evidence. For more about the library and its launch, read the announcement blog . What makes a robot asset SimReady? SimReady Foundation defines what features the OpenUSD asset needs for a simulation use case. Its specifications connect three levels: Profile: a group of features for a use case, such as a robot body. Features: capabilities needed for the use case, such as joints that can be controlled. Requirements: checks on the settings needed for each feature, such as a joint’s drive settings. For this task, those properties include the arm and gripper’s joints and a beverage can asset collisions and mass. Validation checks these settings against the profile’s requirements. The simulation then tests whether the assembled robot can use them to pick up and move the can. What comes with the asset, and what do you add? The UR17G , Robotiq 2F-140 , and beverage can packages include the models and their simulation settings. You assemble the scene and add task code to define the arm–gripper assembly, work surface, starting positions, and controls for moving the arm and opening and closing the gripper. Figure 2. SimReady Central supplies the asset models and simulation settings and the example scene and controls define the pick-and-place task. What should you check before running a pick-and-place task? A robot can look visually correct while stationary in Isaac Sim but move or interact with objects incorrectly when the simulation runs. Before running pick-and-place, test its joints, movement, and contact behavior. You can ask the agent to perform these tests or do them manually in Isaac Sim. Joint settings: Review the arm and gripper’s joint limits and drive settings. Movement: Test a small arm movement and open and close the gripper. Contact: Confirm that the can rests on the work surface without falling through it. During pick-and-place, watch whether a beverage can stay in the gripper as the arm moves. Asset structures vary, so use the settings in your loaded scene as your starting point. We will be going through the overall process of downloading the assets and composing the scene in the steps below. Build a pick-and-place simulation in Isaac Sim This example combines the UR17G arm, Robotiq 2F-140 gripper, and beverage can in Isaac Sim. The task is to grasp the can, lift it, move it to a target, and release it. You can also leverage SimReady Central Space search service endpoint to look for OEM curated content. We will also use a frontier AI model to help create and run the task code in an open Isaac Sim scene. For this example, we use GPT-6 Sol, but another agent and model combination may work if it can load the required skills and execute Python against Isaac Sim (generated code and results can vary). The prompt provides a starting point. Inspect the generated code and check the resulting behavior before adapting the task. Required Software: Install Isaac Sim 6.2, the version used for this example, and check its system requirements. Set up an agent of your choice that can use the Isaac Sim skills. Follow the Agent Skills documentation to make the bundled skills available to your agent. Install the Hugging Face CLI only if you choose the command-line asset download option. Use the USD Search endpoint . Step 1: Download the robot arm, gripper, and beverage can assets Open SimReady Central and find the UR17G arm, Robotiq 2F-140 gripper, and beverage can used here. Select Download on each asset, then use Save to folder or the supplied Hugging Face command. Keep all three complete asset folders intact so Isaac Sim can find their supporting files. Use the asset versions linked in this example and provide your agent with the local USD file paths for the arm, gripper, and beverage can. An example gripper path is shown below; your download location may differ. ~/ASSETS/hf/src/simready-assets-c7fa7615/Robotiq_2F_140/simready_usd/Robotiq_2F_140.usda Figure 3. SimReady Central search and interactive previews help identify the Robotiq 2F-140 gripper and beverage can used in this example. Figure 4. The beverage can’s download options include saving the asset package to a folder or using the Hugging Face CLI. What does asset validation tell you? The arm validation report uses the Robot-Body 4.0.0 profile and the gripper validation report uses Robot-Gripper 3.0.0. Both record passing PhysX driven-joint checks , which inspect joint-drive settings. SimReady profile validation provides a shared baseline for reusing these assets. The pick-and-place run then tests how the arm, gripper, can, and controller work together in the assembled scene. Step 2: Assemble the robot and compose the scene for pick and place With the assets downloaded, use your agent with Isaac Sim skills to help assemble the robot, run validation tools, and create the pick-and-place controls. You can also perform these steps manually using the linked documentation. Start Isaac Sim from its installation directory with the remote Python server enabled so the agent can interact with the simulation through Python: ./isaac-sim.sh -- enable isaacsim.code_editor.python_server If you are using an agent, make sure you start it from the Isaac Sim directory so that it can access the skills needed while going through the steps below. Confirm that all three assets appear without missing-file errors. Ask the agent to inspect the arm and gripper’s joint limits and drive settings, or review them yourself in Isaac Sim. The robot and the gripper contain physics joints which can be tested and validated in the Isaac Sim GUI as well. We will now assemble the arm and the gripper next so that we can control the assembly as a single articulation. You can follow the Robot Assembler tutorial for manual assembly. Here we will ask our agent to complete the assembly and validate it for us: Sample prompt used in this example: Assemble the robot arm <local path to Simready ur17g robot usd>
with the gripper <local path to downloded simready Robotiq_2F_140 gripper usd>
using the Robot Assembly tutorial in Isaac Sim
https://docs.isaacsim.omniverse.nvidia.com/6.2.0/robot_setup/assemble_robots.html. Validate the assembly on completion. The agent ends up using the ‘isaac-sim-remote’ and ‘usd-articulation’ skills packaged with Isaac Sim to complete the assembly and validate the physics of the robot. We now have all the assets needed for running pick and place; the assembled robot and the soda can. We will now proceed with the final portion of the workflow. Figure 5. Joint settings for the UR17G arm and Robotiq 2F-140 gripper in Isaac Sim. With the assembled robot and can in the scene, ask the agent to run the task. Evaluate the simulation behavior using the checks in the next step. Step 3: Test the controls and run pick-and-place Now that the assets include simulation properties and profile validation, we can now test in an assembled scene and controller. The controller coordinates the UR17G arm’s movement with the Robotiq 2F-140 gripper’s opening and closing. Use the behavior checks below to evaluate the agent-generated task.

title: XYBench: Helping with the problem behind the question
abstract: Back to Articles XYBench: Helping with the problem behind the question Enterprise Article Published November 13, 2026 Upvote 4 Kyle Wiggers Ai2Comms Follow allenai 📄 Paper | 🤗 Data | 💻 Code Truly useful AI assistants need to be able to help users who ask misguided questions—not just users who ask the right question with the right amount of detail. We’re releasing XYBench , a benchmark of 8K+ questions that tests how AI assistants respond to requests based on misconceptions, such as asking how to thicken frosting that keeps sliding off cupcakes when the real problem is that the cupcakes are still too warm to frost. XYBench won the Best Resource Paper Award at EMNLP 2026. A mismatch between the approach someone asks about and the goal they want to achieve is known as the XY problem : a person wants to accomplish X, assumes a particular approach Y will work, and asks for help with Y. In the cupcake example, the person is so committed to making the frosting stick that they fail to consider the warmth of the cupcake as the true problem to be addressed. Developed with researchers at Carnegie Mellon, NVIDIA, and Johns Hopkins, XYBench exposes a critical gap in LLMs' ability to troubleshoot problems: recognizing when a user's request is based on an implicit misconception and appropriately redirecting them toward a solution that addresses their actual goal. Drawing on 8,115 real-world questions spanning programming and everyday activities such as cooking and home repair, we introduce a benchmark that measures whether models identify these misconceptions and are able to prioritize effective solutions in their responses. The models we evaluated on XYBench – Claude Sonnet 4.6, GPT-5, Gemini 3.1 Pro, Qwen3.5-9B, and DeepSeek-V4 Pro – often suggested a solution to the user’s problem but kept their answers focused on the original, mistaken approach. Unlike human reference answers, all five models were less likely to steer users away from that approach and toward a solution suited to their goal. People use AI systems with different levels of knowledge and may not always know how best to approach a problem. We hope XYBench helps researchers measure whether model improvements make assistants better at recognizing mistaken assumptions, explaining why a proposed approach might not work, and suggesting more effective alternatives—even when users don't know the right questions to ask. Building XYBench We built XYBench from four sources: 1,557 questions from Stack Overflow, 184 from Stack Exchange, 102 manually curated examples, and 6,272 questions generated from WikiHow guides. For each question, we identified the stated request (Y), what the person explicitly asks for, and the intended request (X)—the underlying goal that can be inferred from context. For the public forum questions, we used the three highest-scored human answers and the accepted answer, where available, to establish the intended request and possible solutions. We filtered out cases where answering the stated request was judged sufficient. For WikiHow, we used Sonnet 4.5 to generate questions around plausible misconceptions in procedural guides, then refined them to include enough context for an expert to infer the underlying goal without stating it outright. We removed examples where answering the literal request would largely resolve the problem. Evaluating how an answer helps A model might spend several paragraphs recommending a more powerful vacuum cleaner, then briefly suggest checking for a clogged hose. If a clog is causing the weak suction, clearing it could solve the problem. A more helpful answer would recognize that the user wants to restore suction and focus on diagnosing the cause. This draws on pragmatics, the branch of linguistics concerned with how context and communicative intent shape meaning. To test whether models use this understanding in their answers, XYBench measures three aspects of each response: Pragmatic solution —records whether a model’s response includes solutions to the stated request (Y) and the intended request (X), checking each separately. Pragmatic emphasis —measures whether a model’s answer focuses on the stated request (Y), focuses on the intended request (X), or balances the two. Misconception identification —measures whether a model’s response steers the user toward the underlying goal (X) while discouraging or avoiding the mistaken approach (Y). In XYBench, Claude Sonnet 4.5 serves as the automated judge. It classifies individual suggestions within each model’s response and assesses the answer’s pragmatic emphasis. To validate Sonnet 4.5’s judgments, two human reviewers independently assessed 500 model responses to XYBench questions. Agreement with the judge, averaged across the reviewers, ranged from 97.5–100% on whether a solution appeared, 84.6–93.3% on misconception identification, and 74.2–79.8% on pragmatic emphasis. What the experiments show We evaluated Sonnet 4.6, GPT-5, Gemini 3.1 Pro, Qwen3.5-9B, and DeepSeek-V4 Pro on XYBench in a single-turn setting, with one response per question. We evaluated human reference answers separately using the same metrics. Across all four sources, every model was more likely to include a solution to the stated request (Y) than to the underlying goal (X). On Stack Overflow, stated-request solutions appeared in 75–86% of responses, compared with 59–71% for underlying-goal solutions. A passing mention of a solution does not make it the focus of an answer. In the vacuum example, a model could briefly suggest unclogging the hose but focus most of its response on buying a more powerful vacuum. We would count that response as containing a solution to the underlying goal, even though the model emphasized the stated request. We measured overall emphasis separately: on Stack Overflow, models focused primarily on the underlying goal in only 35–41% of their responses, and on the stated request in 47–57%. In the remaining responses, models gave similar emphasis to the stated request and the underlying goal. We also tested whether making the user’s goal explicit would help. In an oracle experiment, we supplied both the stated request (Y) and the intended request (X) alongside each question. On Stack Overflow, Sonnet 4.6’s rate of including a solution to the underlying goal rose from 59% to 67%, but its misconception-identification rate fell from 47% to 34%. Across the sources with human reference answers, every model in this experiment still trailed humans on misconception identification. Supplying intent helped, but did not consistently close the gap with human responses. This suggests that detecting intent is only part of the challenge: models also need to act on it when it diverges from the stated request. A separate experiment tested whether models could identify useful advice when judging responses instead of writing them. We gave the same five models, plus GPT-4.1, each question with two possible answers: one focused on the literal request and one explaining the misconception and addressing the underlying goal. On Stack Overflow, all six chose the goal-focused answer in 71–84% of cases. By comparison, only 35–41% of the answers written by the five models in our main evaluation primarily focused on the underlying goal. The results expose a gap between recognizing useful advice and producing it, which a multiple-choice test alone would miss. What this means for evaluation Researchers can use XYBench to test whether changes to prompting or training help models identify misconceptions, offer solutions to users’ underlying problems, and make those solutions the focus of their answers. Measuring each behavior individually lets researchers see whether progress in one also improves the others. Future work could test which training methods help models act on inferred intent—AKA what users need and not just what they literally asked for.

title: llama.cpp v1.0.0 : A stronger foundation for the local AI ecosystem
abstract: Back to Articles llama.cpp v1.0.0 : A stronger foundation for the local AI ecosystem Team Article Published November 13, 2026 Upvote 125 +119 Daniel Bevenius danbev Follow ggml-org Georgi Gerganov ggerganov Follow ggml-org merve merve Follow ggml-org llama.cpp makes it possible to run multi-modal LLMs across a wide range of hardware - from consumer-grade local machines to high-end enterprise servers. Through quantization, optimized backends, and a portable C/C++ implementation, we make AI inference accessible at every level of the software stack. We believe this is the most lightweight, versatile and sensible platform for building cross-platform and private AI products. During the 3.5 years since its inception , the project has grown a lot and many downstream applications already depend on our work. We expect this trend to continue as local AI and privacy become increasingly important in our everyday lives. Every new integration means more developers depending on our library interfaces and therefore having a flexible but stable API is paramount. Today we release libraries v1.0.0 , highlighting our responsibility to those developers. Moving forward, both llama.cpp and ggml will reflect API and ABI incompatibilities with major-version bumps. As adoption grows, we will be stricter about making those boundaries visible to downstream consumers. Releases Release Library Public header(s) llama.cpp v1.0.0 - LLM inference in C/C++ libllama llama.cpp/include/ ggml v1.0.0 - Tensor library for machine learning libggml ggml/include/ Semantic version update rules The following rules apply to all ggml-org projects using semantic versioning : Change type Bump MAJOR Breaking change to the public C API in ./include MINOR Backward-compatible feature, backend updates, model support, or API addition PATCH Bug fix with no API change Distribution We are looking forward to expanding the ways in which ggml-org software is distributed and reaches developers and end-users. For more information about how to add ggml-org projects to your packaging and release pipelines, please check the following discussion . Channel Platforms Pre-release artifacts Linux, macOS, Windows, Android, iOS Docker Linux Debian Linux Homebrew macOS, Linux conda-forge Windows, macOS, Linux MacPorts macOS Winget Windows XCFramework iOS, macOS Development The project has fostered an amazing open-source community with highly-skilled and talented contributors. With the rapid advance of AI capabilities in the field of software engineering, we continue to adapt and integrate LLMs in our developement cycle in a thoughtful and resonable manner. Maintaining a high quality codebase, staying in control of the architecture and understanding the implementation details will remain our top priorities. To reinforce the faster pace of development we continue to invest more and more resources in improving the CI infrastructure behind the projects. Thanks to HF technologies such as HF Buckets and HF Jobs we are able to scale the capacity necessary to guarantee correctness for every change that lands on the master branches. With hardware support from NVIDIA, AMD, Qualcomm, Arm, IBM and Intel, we continue to enroll more self-hosted runners across all major hardware platforms. Backend and model coverage The underlying machine learning engine of llama.cpp - ggml is designed to run on virtually any hardware in existence. This is achieved by implementing dedicated ggml backends. Each backend can be compiled as a dynamic library and optionally loaded at runtime. A complete list of the currently implemented backends can be found here . We are committed to provide continuous support of all model architectures. Currently, llama.cpp supports more than 150 architecture variants as well as all mainstream speculative decoding methods. Thanks The llama.cpp team at Hugging Face is thankful for the incredible support from the community. Special thanks to the long-time maintainers of the project and all contributors . This is a significant milestone which would not have been possible without our joint efforts! Additional resources llama.cpp examples ggml-org at Hugging Face ggml-org at Github Check out Llama desktop apps for MacOS and Windows, shipped with love by the team behind llama.cpp and Hugging Face.

title: Best AI Video Generation Models in 2026: Elo, Price per Second, Open Weights
abstract: The AI video leaderboard looks very different from 12 months ago. Native audio is now table stakes. Clips run 15–30 seconds. And an open-weights model sits in the top 3. This ranking (as of Nov 13, 2026) uses one quality signal: blind human-preference Elo from the Artificial Analysis Video Arena . We pair it with API price per second and the license status of the weights. You can check the deployment options and specs here through our GPULeaderboard.com chrome extension . Quality : Artificial Analysis ranks models by Elo from blind pairwise votes by validated evaluators . Each vote compares 2 clips from the same prompt. We rank by the AA-Video-T2V v2.1 (with audio) board. We also report the AA-Video-I2V v2.1 score. Anchor : Kling 3.0 1080p (Pro) is fixed at 1000 Elo on both boards. A score below 1000 means voters preferred Kling 3.0 more often. Price : Artificial Analysis lists cost per minute on each creator’s API. It normalizes to 1080p where offered. We divide by 60 to get price per second. Vendor rates at 720p are often lower, and we flag those gaps. Confidence : Most top-10 scores carry a ±13 to ±15 Elo interval. Models within ~25 points are statistically close. Treat ranks 3–8 as a cluster, not a strict order. Source: Artificial Analysis T2V and I2V leaderboards, retrieved November 13, 2026. $/sec = AA per-minute price ÷ 60. “H3 post-train” means the model was fine-tuned from MiniMax H3’s weights. Wan 3.0 holds the top text-to-video spot with 7,651 votes behind it. Alibaba launched it on August 24, 2026 . It generates 30-second 1080p clips from text, PDFs and slide decks, priced at $0.20 per second. The document-to-video input is the differentiator. You can hand it a deck and get a structured video back. The trade-off is openness. There are no downloadable weights for Wan 3.0 . Wan 2.2 (July 2025) remains Alibaba’s last open video flagship . Note the I2V gap too: Wan 3.0 drops to 11th on image-to-video. Best for: long single takes, explainer videos from existing documents. Utopai X is the only model in the top 2 on both boards. Utopai Studios, a Mountain View film studio, built it by post-training MiniMax H3 . It beats the base H3 it came from. Access runs only through Utopai’s PAI platform. PAI charges 93 credits per second , with plans starting at $15 for 1,000 credits. Developers cannot call it from a pipeline. Best for: filmmakers working inside a studio tool. Not for programmatic use. H3 is the first open-weights model in the video top tier. MiniMax launched the API on July 31, 2026 and published weights on August 3 . It is a 33B dense single-stream Transformer, using Qwen3-VL-32B as its encoder . It outputs video with native 32 kHz stereo audio. Read the license before you download. The Hugging Face weights carry real limits: Even so, H3 has become the base layer of 2026 video. Utopai X, HeyGen Video 1, fal’s H3 Max and Pika H3 Flex are all post-trains of it. AA also lists Pruna’s P-Video-2-Pro as a MiniMax collaboration. Best for: teams outside excluded regions that want to fine-tune a frontier video model. Seedance 2.5 leads image-to-video. ByteDance began rolling it out on July 31, 2026 through Jimeng AI and Doubao Pro. It supports up to 30-second generations with up to 30 image, 10 video and 10 audio references . Pricing needs care. AA lists $34.12 per minute, the highest on the board. BytePlus lists $1.156 for a 5-second 720p clip without video input , or about $0.23/sec. Confirm API access in your region before planning around it. Best for: reference-heavy, image-led ad and character work. Gemini Omni Flash 1.2 is the newest entry, generally available since November 5, 2026 . It added 3–15 second clips and a 30% price cut over version 1.1. Video output costs $12 per 1M tokens, about $0.070 per second at 720p . It jumped 27 Elo over Omni Flash 1.1 on text-to-video. Requests to 1.1 route to 1.2 from December 3, 2026 . Best for: teams already on the Gemini API who want a top-5 model under $0.11/sec. fal Research post-trained FLUX 3 Max with Black Forest Labs , launching it October 19, 2026. fal says a 10-second 720p clip renders in about 12 seconds . Seedance 2.5 took 277.80 seconds in fal’s own comparison. It shares an API with fal’s H3 Max. Switching between them takes a single model-ID change. Best for: latency-sensitive pipelines and rapid iteration. HeyGen Video 1 is a general scene generator, not an avatar engine. It is a post-train of MiniMax H3 . It leads the silent (audio-off) text-to-video board at 1146 Elo. At $0.04 per second, it costs half of base H3 for a similar score. The API model ID is heygen-video-1 . Best for: high-volume social clips and ad variants where discard rate drives cost. fal Research post-trained H3 Max on the open MiniMax H3 base . It focused on prompt adherence and visual quality. fal claims it renders a 5-second clip in about 3 seconds . It briefly led image-to-video after its August 2026 launch. Newer post-trains have since passed it. Best for: fal users who want H3 quality without self-hosting. SkyReels V4 dates from March 2026 yet still ranks top-5 on image-to-video. At $0.35 per second, it is hard to justify on text-to-video. Gemini Omni Flash 1.2 scores higher for less than a third of the price. FLUX 3 is BFL’s first video model, with 20-second clips and native audio . One backbone also handles robot action prediction. BFL says it will release open-weight versions later this year . Until FLUX 3 Dev ships, treat it as API-only. MiniMax H3 family : Pika H3 Flex shipped October 29, 2026. It cuts H3 to 6 sampling steps . Local inference still needs an H100 80GB and about 215 GB of downloads. Video Rebirth’s HyperFlow H3 Flash compresses H3 to 13.7B. It runs from a 9.1 GB GGUF on a 24 GB GPU. Its sibling, Hyperflow H3, ranks #7 on image-to-video at 1120 Elo. LTX-2.5 : Lightricks released the 22B model on August 11, 2026 . It adds native multishot generation and joint audio. Under the license, entities with $10M+ annual revenue need a paid license . It trails the H3 family by roughly 200 Elo. But it gates by revenue, not territory. For US and EU teams, that makes it a practical default. See our LTX-2.5 launch coverage . Apache 2.0 options : Wan 2.2 and HunyuanVideo 1.5 remain the go-to picks for permissive licensing or a single consumer GPU. Neither appears on the current AA boards. Quality and price no longer track each other. The 3 cheapest top-tier models are all H3 derivatives or H3 itself. Value = (Elo − 1000) ÷ price per second. Higher is better. Illustrative only; it ignores resolution and clip-length differences. At the top, Wan 3.0 buys you about 23 Elo over HeyGen Video 1. It costs 5x more per second. Whether that matters depends on how many takes you discard. The post Best AI Video Generation Models in 2026: Elo, Price per Second, Open Weights appeared first on MarkTechPost .

title: Perplexity Releases Decider v1.3: Open-Weight Decision Models Add Locate
abstract: Perplexity has released pplx-decider-v1.3 and pplx-decider-flash-v1.3 , the latest versions of its open-weight decision models. Perplexity Decider v1.3 is a decision model that returns probabilities, not generated text. It answers yes/no, multiple-choice and score questions about a text or image input. The main addition is Locate, which extracts exact text spans by type or instruction. Weights ship under Apache 2.0 on Hugging Face . Both models also run in the Perplexity Decisions API and on OpenRouter . You can check the deployment options and specs here through our GPULeaderboard.com chrome extension . Decider is Perplexity’s family of decision models, inspired by TypeSafe’s Jev . Each request has a shared ‘state’ plus one or more questions with labeled options. The model returns a probability per option instead of writing an answer. v1.3 succeeds v1.2 and Flash v1.2 . Flash v1.3 is distilled from the large model. Perplexity adapts a generative LLM backbone into a classifier. The output layer starts from the base model’s LM head, pruned to option tokens (A, B, C). A linear decision head reads the hidden state at a <|marker|> token and outputs option probabilities. Full-attention layers are made bidirectional, which Perplexity’s ablations showed helps. v1.3 also changes attention between questions. In v1.2, every question saw every other question, so answers could shift. In v1.3, the state sees all questions, but each question sees only the state and itself. All questions about one input still run in a single forward pass. Weights are averaged across 3 seeds. Flash is trained by minimizing KL divergence to the large model’s outputs. Locate returns exact text spans with start and end character offsets. Fields can be short labels (‘location’) or instructions (‘Extract the city name where the job is located.’). It targets NER, PII detection and extractive QA. A new <|locate|> token is added per requested field. A span head plus a LoRA adapter is trained, while the backbone and decision head stay frozen. The adapter stays unmerged because merging hurt decision accuracy. All results below are self-reported by Perplexity : Benchmark rows are Perplexity’s self-reported numbers from its launch post . The API endpoint is POST https://api.perplexity.ai/v1/decisions . Model IDs are pplx-decider-v1.3 and pplx-decider-flash-v1.3 , with -latest aliases. Pricing is $0.02 and $0.01 per 1M input tokens. Output is free. Perplexity’s latency test put an ~243K-token request at 16s on v1.3 and 5s on Flash. Locate requests allow up to 128 questions. Locally, load the model with Decider.from_pretrained() from the pplx_decider package. Full-attention layers must run noncausally. Perplexity recommends v1.3 for nuanced rubrics and Flash for high-volume routing. Check out the technical details , Decider v1.3 model card , Flash v1.3 model card and API docs . You can check the deployment options and specs here through our GPULeaderboard.com chrome extension . title: Google Releases TPU Sync: Open-Source KV Cache Transfer for TPUs
abstract: Google Cloud has released TPU Sync , an open-source C++ library for moving KV caches and model weights on Cloud TPUs. The Google TPU Sync KV cache transfer library treats TPU HBM, host DRAM, shared storage and the data center network as one memory hierarchy. It targets a growing bottleneck: moving model state, not computing it. Google reports over 90% lower KV transfer latency on 235B to 480B parameter MoE models. TPU Sync is an open-source C++ library from Google that moves TPU-tiled tensors across memory tiers with asynchronous DMA. It handles 2 jobs: KV cache state during inference, and trainer-to-sampler weight broadcast in reinforcement learning (RL). The repository is licensed Apache-2.0. The library spans TPU HBM, pinned host DRAM, shared storage and multi-host DCN. Storage uses experimental POSIX backends, including local SSDs and Google Cloud Managed Lustre. Google lists 4 design choices: Above this sit a global KV store for prefix lookups, a transfer controller and a KV cache manager. The prefill node offloads KV blocks to pinned host RAM through async DMA. The controller streams them host-to-host to the assigned decode node. Arriving blocks move into decode-node HBM while decoding continues. Google ran internal tests in July 2026 on TPU v7x (2x2x1). The stack was tpu-inference v0.24.0, JAX 0.10.2 and libtpu 0.0.42.1. Google team states that real-world results will vary. For P/D disaggregated serving: TPU Sync integrates with PyTorch through TorchTPU and with JAX natively. In vLLM-TorchTPU , it is the TPU KV connector behind vLLM’s KVConnector interface. In SGLang-TorchTPU , it is the P/D transfer backend and hierarchical cache I/O backend. On GKE, llm-d 1.0 uses it for prefix-cache-affinity routing and experimental spill to Managed Lustre. Inferact and RadixArk co-engineered the vLLM and SGLang integrations. Google says Meta and Wayfair are evaluating the architecture. The bandwidth figures measure different paths. TPU Sync’s number is host PCIe DMA. Mooncake’s number is network transfer over RoCE. Check out the technical blog , the GitHub repo , vLLM-TorchTPU and SGLang-TorchTPU . title: Google Releases Gemini 4 Hydrogen: 2.5x Faster Than Gemini 3.8 Flash
abstract: Google has released Gemini 4 Hydrogen , a fast model for coding and agentic work. Gemini 4 Hydrogen is a proprietary model from Google DeepMind built for everyday agent loops. It sits below the frontier models Gemini 4 Carbon and Gemini 4 Argon . Google calls it its “daily driver for agentic workflows.” Hydrogen is a closed-weights model served through the Gemini API and Google products. The model card says it is adapted from Gemini 4 Carbon. Google does not disclose parameter count, architecture or training hardware. The knowledge cutoff is March 2026. Input covers text, images, audio, video, PDFs, tables and charts, per the What’s New guide . Output is text. The 1M window is shared by input, thinking and output tokens. Developers set thinking_level inside generation_config . Values are low , medium , high and a new xhigh . The default is high , not medium as on 3.8 Flash. A minimal setting now returns an error. The model card warns that higher levels use more tokens. The key design idea is role-splitting across models. In Google Antigravity , an Orchestrator option switches models inside 1 task. Carbon explores, resolves ambiguity and plans. Hydrogen edits files, updates packages and runs tests. When Hydrogen hits friction, it hands control back to Carbon. On Terminal-Bench 4.1, this pairing reached near-Carbon task success rates. It used 24% less quota and finished 19% faster than Carbon alone. The Antigravity SDK exposes the same split for custom multi-agent systems. All figures are self-reported by Google unless noted. Speed is the headline claim. Hydrogen finishes tasks 2.5x faster than 3.8 Flash at the default high level. In partner tests, it ran 2x to 2.8x faster with 12% to 23% fewer tokens. Google also reports more than 5x fewer fabricated claims than 3.8 Flash. It scored 96.7% on an internal agent honesty evaluation. It was 2.3x more resilient to indirect prompt injection on Gray Swan’s benchmark. The API price is $1.50 per 1M input tokens and $7.50 per 1M output tokens. Pricing is flat across the full window. Output pricing includes thinking tokens. Implicit caching cuts input to $0.075 per 1M for prompts of 4,096 tokens or more. Explicit caching is not supported. The price context matters. Gemini 3.8 Flash costs $0.75/$3.75 until December 31, 2026. From January 1, 2027, it rises to $1.50/$7.50, matching Hydrogen. Argon costs $2/$10 until November 30, 2026, then $4/$20. The model ID is gemini-4-hydrogen . It is live in the Gemini API, Google AI Studio on all tiers, and Android Studio. It also ships in Gemini for business , the Gemini app, Google Search and Sheets. Antigravity access requires Google AI Pro or Ultra. Vertex AI is not mentioned in the launch posts. Migration from 3.8 Flash needs a few changes. Remove temperature , top_p and top_k , since the server ignores them. Remove cached_content fields. Raise hardcoded max_output_tokens caps to 65,536. Terminal-Bench 4.0 and 4.1 are different versions, so cross-version scores are not directly comparable. Check out the launch post , the model card , the developer post and the What’s New guide . title: Liquid AI Releases LiquidCodec, a 74M-Parameter Streaming Audio Codec
abstract: Liquid AI has released LiquidCodec , the audio codec behind its LFM3-Audio-2B and LFM3-Omni-2B models. The LiquidCodec audio codec is a ~74M-parameter streaming speech tokenizer. It turns speech into tokens a language model can predict, then converts those tokens back into audio. Liquid AI had 2 goals: easy-to-predict tokens and fast conversion back to speech. The weights are on Hugging Face . LiquidCodec is a Liquid AI speech codec that compresses 24 kHz audio into 12 token streams. Each 80 ms frame becomes 12 discrete tokens, per the LFM3-Audio-2B model card . It replaces Kyutai’s Mimi , which Liquid AI used in LFM2-Audio-1.5B. Mimi has 96.2M parameters. The pipeline is encode, quantize, decode. Liquid AI uses blocks from its LFM3 architecture in both the encoder and decoder. The 2 halves are symmetric, and the encoder is fully causal, which suits streaming. Quantization uses grouped finite scalar quantization (GFSQ) instead of residual vector quantization (RVQ). In RVQ, each codebook encodes what the previous one missed. GFSQ groups are independent, so all 12 codebooks can be predicted in parallel by MaskGIT-style transformers. The decoder predicts spectral coefficients directly. This avoids learned transposed-convolution upsampling, a common cost in waveform decoders. Training ran in 2 stages. Stage 1 used 264,000 hours of speech across 107 languages. It applied waveform and spectral losses, without adversarial losses. Stage 2 fine-tuned on 55,000 hours of full-band speech (24 kHz or higher) with adversarial critics. Liquid AI says this removed metallic artifacts left after stage 1. A final decoder-only quantization-aware training (QAT) step targets edge inference. Liquid AI measured speed in FP32 on 1 CPU thread of an Apple M4 Max MacBook Pro. LiquidCodec ran at ~361x real time for encoding and ~87x for decoding. These are self-reported figures. Real-time factor (RTF) is processing time divided by audio length, so lower is better. LiquidCodec’s encode RTF is 0.0028, against 0.0361 for Mimi, 0.2145 for NanoCodec and 0.7359 for X-Codec 2. Decode RTF is 0.0115, against 0.0329, 0.2543 and 0.0379. That is about 13x lower encode RTF and 2.9x lower decode RTF than Mimi. Liquid AI used 8 test sets. These were LibriSpeech test-clean, Seed-TTS English and Mandarin, and 5 FLEURS languages (German, French, Mandarin, Japanese, Korean). Baselines were X-Codec 2, NanoCodec and Mimi at 12 codebooks. *Measured by Liquid AI in its LiquidCodec blog . Mimi measured at 12 codebooks. The codec loads through Hugging Face Transformers with trust_remote_code=True . Call encode() to get audio codes and decode() to get a waveform. A native LiquidCodecStreamingCache supports chunk-by-chunk decoding, per the model card . The card’s examples use CUDA with bfloat16. For edge use, Liquid AI lists Q4_0, Q4_K_M and Q8_0 GGUF builds for llama.cpp. GGUF repos ship with LFM3-Audio-2B and LFM3-Omni-2B . Q4_0 with decoder-only QAT shrinks the decoder footprint by 3.5x. LibriSpeech ViSQOL dips only from 4.319 to 4.292. Check out the technical blog , the model weights on Hugging Face , and LFM3-Audio-2B and LFM3-Omni-2B .
