title: Chinese frontier AI models carry the fingerprint of export-controlled GPUs
abstract:
Top Chinese Frontier AI Models Carry the Fingerprint of Export-Controlled NVIDIA Blackwell GPUs Will DePue November 12, 2026 Print / save PDF Cite this report Executive Summary Our forensic analysis of publicly released AI models finds evidence that DeepSeek, Moonshot AI, MiniMax and Ant Group have gained access to NVIDIA’s Blackwell GPUs, despite restrictions on exporting these chips to China, and are using that hardware to create their AI models. Six models released by these companies since April 2026 contain numerical patterns matching Blackwell hardware, whereas earlier models from the same companies match NVIDIA’s older Hopper generation. The findings suggest that several leading Chinese AI developers have begun using Blackwell to train their newest models. U.S. officials and press reports had already alleged that DeepSeek and Moonshot AI were using Blackwell chips, without publishing technical evidence. The evidence comes entirely from the models’ own published weights, rather than from leaks or insider accounts. We recover traces of the models’ initial values, and then search for the hardware configurations and initial configurations that reproduce them; for DeepSeek-V4-Flash and Kimi K3, we also confirmed the match on physical Blackwell chips. The fingerprint identifies how the weights were created and supports, without proving, the inference that Blackwell also performed the training. Specially configured AMD hardware, which is also restricted from export to China, is the only alternative we have identified; we have excluded it for DeepSeek-V4-Flash, and consider it very unlikely for the other five models. Notably, our findings provide technical evidence of access to advanced computing hardware, but do not establish where the chips were located, how access was obtained, or whether export controls were violated. Table 1. Hardware fingerprints in successive models from DeepSeek, Moonshot AI, MiniMax and Ant Group Link ↗ Lab Model Released Chip the model was started on DeepSeek DeepSeek-V3 Dec 2024 NVIDIA Hopper (lab disclosed H800) DeepSeek-V4-Flash Apr 2026 • NVIDIA Blackwell B200/B300 DeepSeek-V4-Pro Apr 2026 • NVIDIA Blackwell GB200/GB300 Moonshot AI Kimi K2 Jul 2025 NVIDIA Hopper (lab disclosed H800) Kimi K2.5 Jan 2026 NVIDIA Hopper (lab disclosed H800) Kimi K3 Jul 2026 • NVIDIA Blackwell GB200/GB300 Kimi K3.1-Pro Nov 2026 • NVIDIA Blackwell GB200/GB300 MiniMax MiniMax-M2.7 Apr 2026 NVIDIA Hopper MiniMax-M3 Jun 2026 • NVIDIA Blackwell B200/B300 Ant Group Ling-3.0-flash Aug 2026 NVIDIA Hopper Ling-3.1-flash Oct 2026 • NVIDIA Blackwell GB200/GB300 • Requires a U.S. license for export to China; none have been reported. A Hopper fingerprint cannot distinguish an H800 from an H100 SXM or H200; the H800 identifications above are lab disclosures, not findings of this method. Full list of models in Appendix 2 ↓ Main Findings Six models from four Chinese labs read as Blackwell-trained. DeepSeek-V4-Flash and MiniMax-M3 match NVIDIA’s Blackwell-class B200 or B300 chips, which have 148 processor cores (called streaming multiprocessors , or SMs). DeepSeek-V4-Pro, Kimi K3, Kimi K3.1-Pro and Ling-3.1-flash match the GB200 or GB300 chips, also Blackwell-class, which have 152 processor cores. Kimi K3.1-Pro starts from the same seed as K3, and may be a checkpoint of K3 with further post-training. Chinese labs started training on Blackwell relatively recently. DeepSeek’s models read as Hopper-trained through DeepSeek-V3 (released in December 2024), and as Blackwell from DeepSeek V4 (released in April 2026). Moonshot’s models read as Hopper through Kimi K2.5 (January 2026) and as Blackwell from K3 (July 2026). One Moonshot model sits in between: Kimi K2.7-Code, posted six weeks before K3, is built on the Hopper-era weights but contains a small part that matches the B200 or B300. MiniMax’s models read as Hopper through M2.7 (April 2026) and as Blackwell from M3 (June 2026). Ant Group’s Ling-3.0-flash (August 2026) reads as Hopper, while its Ling-3.1-flash (October 2026) reads as Blackwell. The Hopper readings do not identify a specific chip: H800s, H100 SXMs and H200s share the same fingerprint. Not every Chinese AI lab has switched to Blackwell. The newest models we could read from Alibaba (Qwen), Zhipu (GLM), Tencent, Xiaomi and StepFun all read as Hopper-trained. Meituan says its LongCat-2.0 was trained entirely on “AI ASIC superpods,” and we found no NVIDIA fingerprint in the model weights it’s released. The method gets known answers right. For 24 specific models, the developer has publicly said what hardware was used. In every case, our method agrees with the public announcement. NVIDIA’s own Nemotron-3 Ultra, whose technical report names the GB200 for one phase of its training, reads as 152 SMs, the same as Kimi K3. The matches are far stronger than chance would explain. Even unrelated numbers can appear to match when enough combinations are tried. Across the roughly 6 trillion seed-and-layout combinations in our search, the strongest chance match would be expected to reach about 8 sigma—a measure of how far a result stands above ordinary random variation. The strongest evidence for each of the six models ranges from 49 to 1,385 sigma. Even the weakest individual test we report reaches 20 sigma. The training runs were data-center scale. From each model’s size and the amount of data it was trained on, we estimate that the two largest runs, Kimi K3 and DeepSeek-V4-Pro, each needed thousands of Blackwell GPUs for two to three months, assuming each model was trained on the hardware that initialized it. Our best estimates are about 4,500 and 3,000, the equivalent of about 11,500 and 7,500 H100s, the previous-generation NVIDIA chip in which AI training clusters are commonly sized, and about 12,000 Blackwell GPUs across the five runs (Table 2). At roughly $70,000 per GPU—the cost implied by a Wall Street Journal report that about 36,000 Blackwell chips being installed in Malaysia for ByteDance’s use would cost more than $2.5 billion—the largest of these clusters would cost roughly $200 million to $300 million, and the five together more than half a billion dollars. These figures cover only the final training runs; the labs’ total spending on export-controlled GPUs is likely in the billions of dollars. Table 2. Rough scale of each training run Link ↗ Model H100 equivalents Blackwell GPUs, best estimate Blackwell range Estimated run length DeepSeek-V4-Flash 3,500 1,500 250–5,000 50 days DeepSeek-V4-Pro 7,500 3,000 750–6,500 70 days Kimi K3 11,500 4,500 1,000–9,500 70 days MiniMax-M3 3,500 1,500 200–7,000 60 days Ling-3.1-flash 4,000 1,500 400–6,500 100 days All five 30,000 12,000 7,000–22,000 Each estimate is a run’s training compute divided by what one Blackwell GPU delivers over the run, rounded to the nearest 500. Training compute is about six operations per active parameter for every training token, plus attention. We assume the GPUs ran at about 20% of their peak speed, in line with other disclosed Blackwell training runs (25% for DeepSeek, which has reported 39% for its previous model), and for the run lengths shown, which we estimate from release timelines. H100 equivalents convert at NVIDIA’s published peak speeds: a B200 or B300 equals about 2.3 H100s, and a GB200 or GB300 about 2.5. We are not confident in these estimates. They rest on assumptions that the weights cannot confirm: how efficiently each lab used its GPUs (often called MFU), which no lab has published for these runs; how many tokens each model was trained on (DeepSeek’s counts are its own, and we take them on trust; the others are our estimates, made from the weights by a method we have not yet published); how long each run lasted, which no lab has stated; and that training stayed on the hardware that created the weights. Run length matters most, because halving it doubles the GPU count.

title: Edge0-145B: Frontier AI Capabilities on Your Own Computer
abstract:
Today, we're open-sourcing Edge0-145B and Edge0-120B , together with our unified inference framework and deployment tools. Edge0-145B is the world's first open-source on-device AI model with 145 billion parameters. It brings coding, reasoning, and agent capabilities that rival frontier cloud models to your own computer. On-device AI has long forced a tradeoff between model capability and what the hardware can run. Larger models demand more memory, bandwidth, and power; smaller models can struggle with complex work. Moving that work to the cloud adds model-provider fees, data-handling constraints, and a dependence on connectivity. This release addresses those constraints in four ways: The constraint What Edge0-145B makes possible Large models are difficult to run on personal hardware. A 145B model runs locally on a compatible laptop, with reported peak memory of 29GB and decoding above 80 tokens/s. Small on-device models can fall short on demanding tasks. Coding, reasoning, and instruction-following results are competitive with specific frontier cloud models, as the comparisons below show. A useful assistant needs to finish work, not just answer questions. The model plans, writes and runs code, debugs errors, and checks results visually for projects such as 3D scenes, games, hardware programs, and PCB designs. Cloud workflows bring recurring fees, sensitive-data restrictions, and network dependence. Local inference incurs no corresponding cloud-model token or API fees; data can stay on the computer, and core capabilities keep working offline. Hardware and electricity still cost money. We're releasing the full stack so developers can reproduce the results, evaluate or fine-tune the models, and integrate them into their own products. Get the model weights , explore the inference framework , or try the Edge0 App . How We Make 100B+ Parameter AI Run on a Personal Computer Edge0-145B Laptop Performance: Memory, Speed, and Power Edge0-145B makes a 145-billion-parameter model usable on a personal laptop. A useful local model has to fit in memory, process prompts promptly, generate fast enough to use, and keep power consumption under control. It also needs to sustain longer tasks. Requirement Reported Edge0-145B result What it enables Memory 29GB peak memory Runs on a compatible personal laptop, such as a MacBook Pro, without a server. Prompt processing 1,100+ tokens/s prefill Processes long prompts, including dozens of pages of code, before generation begins. Generation 80+ tokens/s decode Generates faster than a person reads. Power Approximately 120W typical power Sustains operation without throttling in the reported setup. Long tasks 128K–256K context Maintains essentially the same speed on long inputs, supporting extended work. Our earlier Edge0-35B phone release reported peak memory below 2.5GB. On an iPhone 18 Pro Max, Edge0-35B delivers 37+ tokens/s using approximately 2.5GB of memory. Edge0-145B has roughly four times as many parameters; its laptop comparison reports 80+ tokens/s and 28GB peak memory. These measurements apply to different models and hardware. On-device model scale over time. The chart covers 67 open models of at least 1B parameters from 14 labs, intended for phones, laptops, and AI PCs. Same-size base, instruct, and reasoning variants count once; each line tracks a lab's largest model, including releases before July 2025. Filled points mark new highs and hollow points other releases. The scale is logarithmic below 40B and linear above it. Apple is excluded because its weights are not released. Sources: vendor announcements and model cards. Why On-Device Models Have Stayed Small Memory limits kept most on-device models below 10B parameters before September 2026. Apple Intelligence's on-device foundation model had approximately 3B parameters, while Google's Gemini Nano came in 1.8B and 3.25B versions. Even a 7B model could consume approximately 4GB of memory. Larger models faced a memory wall. Model weights occupy storage and must be read during generation, competing for limited memory and bandwidth with the operating system and other apps. Even an aggressively compressed 35B model could need approximately 20GB of memory, far more than a phone could make available. Compute, bandwidth, and power created competing constraints. Larger models offered more capability, but strained memory capacity, generation speed, and battery life. Making models smaller helped them fit, often at the cost of capability. Privacy alone could not close that gap. Apple Intelligence protected user data, but Apple acknowledged that its on-device model was not designed for agentic applications requiring general world knowledge. The prevailing assumption was that on-device intelligence could not match the cloud. Under the Hood of Edge0: Four Layers of Model and Inference Design We designed Edge0-145B and its inference engine together to reduce the memory and data movement that make large models difficult to run locally. The design spans architecture, training, loading, and scheduling. Architecture: share large matrices across sparse experts. Sharing matrices substantially reduces the weights that must be stored and moved while keeping the expert count unchanged. Each group of 64 experts shares two large matrices, while each expert retains a small set of parameters that captures its differences. Previously, every expert stored a complete set of matrices. Of the model's 145B total parameters, only approximately 10B participate in computation on each inference step. Training: build for local execution from day one. We train the model in its on-device architecture from the outset, with deployment constraints built into its design. This avoids treating local deployment as a compression or pruning step after training a cloud model. Loading: pipeline GPU memory, system memory, and SSD access. Reading and computation overlap across three storage tiers, avoiding serial waits. Frequently used “hot experts” remain in GPU memory. An expert library of approximately 40GB sits in system memory, with experts brought into GPU memory as needed. Approximately 48GB of vocabulary data resides on the SSD and is read on demand. Scheduling: use the CPU and GPU together. The GPU computes cached experts while the CPU handles the remaining work in parallel. Speculative decoding verifies multiple candidate tokens at once, spreading the cost of reading weights across more output tokens. These choices support the reported 80+ tokens/s decode rate. Model and inference-engine design work together to make 100B+ parameter inference practical on personal computers. Source: internal testing. Together, these changes let parameter counts grow from tens of billions to more than a hundred billion without proportional increases in memory use, power consumption, and latency. What Edge0 Can Do: Anything From Chat to Complex Work on Your Computer Edge0-145B can carry a complex task through to a usable result. Its coding and reasoning capabilities support local workflows that combine planning, tool use, execution, debugging, and visual checks. The benchmarks establish its capabilities; the demonstrations show how it puts them to work. Coding and reasoning that rival frontier cloud models Edge0-145B is competitive with specific frontier cloud models across coding, reasoning, knowledge, and instruction following: Coding: It scores 64.6 on DeepSWE 1.1 , ahead of Qwen3.8-Flash-Next at 58.7 and DeepSeek-V4-Flash-0731 at 54.4. Reasoning and knowledge: It scores 90.4 on GPQA-Diamond , close to DeepSeek-V4-Flash-0731 at 90.8 and Claude-Opus-4.6 \(Max\) at 91.3. Instruction following: It scores 80.6 on IFBench , ahead of DeepSeek-V4-Flash-0731 at 79.2 and Claude-Opus-4.6 \(Max\) at 62.5. Its 86.52 on Terminal-Bench 2.1 also exceeds Qwen3.8-Flash-Next's 83.3, DeepSeek-V4-Flash-0731's 82.7, and Claude's 78.2. On AA-LCR, Edge0-145B scores 79.3 to Claude's 78.0.

title: AI is turning Apple's app review process into a nightmare for synth developers
abstract:
The surge of AI-generated apps is overwhelming Apple’s app review process, leaving developers caught in the crossfire – two examples among many. A flood of new iOS apps has emerged over the last few months. An estimated 10–20 new iOS music apps enter the market every day. This is because AI now makes it possible for anyone to vibe code their own apps and AUv3 plugins. However, getting an app into the Apple App Store requires going through the app review process. AI has affected not only the number of new releases per day but also Apple’s holy app review process, creating more nightmares than joy for many developers. What Is The Apple App Review Process? Developing and releasing a VST plugin is simple. You set up a website, upload your installers, set a price, and you’re good to go. It’s more complicated on iOS. To publish an app, you must first join the Apple Developer Program, which costs $99 per year. As a member, you can submit apps with AUv3 support, but they won’t become available immediately. Whether they are hand-coded or created with the help of AI, all apps must go through Apple’s review process. Every app, whether a synthesizer, effects, game, or utility app, must first get through this barrier. This process verifies that the app meets requirements, including security standards. That’s a major advantage over many new, freely available VST plugins . You can be confident that everything you download to your iOS or macOS device has been checked and is free of anything suspicious. So far, the process from submission to release has taken 24 to 48 hours, and sometimes a few days. Developers say the typical review takes a day or two. Apple’s own App Review guidelines state: App Review works around the clock, typically reviewing at least 50% of submissions in less than 24 hours and 90% in less than 48 hours.” AI And The Impact Of The Apple App Review Process 24-48 days or a few days! That’s what most developers are currently dreaming of. The Apple App Review process is currently on the verge of collapsing due to the flood of new iOS apps (AI or not), or even hallucinating, if you ask iOS developers. Various developers, including AudioThing, Igor Vasiliev, Sugar Bytes, and others, say their new apps have been stuck in App Review for weeks rather than days, with no updates. As a result, many releases focused on cross-platform compatibility are currently struggling. Take Pittsburgh Modular , for example: their new Microvolt 3901 synth was released as a VST on October 27th, while the iOS version only arrived today, November 12th. However, they planned a simultaneous release. Igor Vasiliev ‘s new HollowTone app (go check out that brilliant app!) also spent weeks stuck in the review process. Most developers can handle a few delays, provided the app is good and ultimately gets purchased. The problem arises when the app review process becomes erratic—or stops accepting the app altogether—even though it’s just another synth. Some developers have reported this. Unfiltered Audio Sinusoidal Run Rhythm Unfiltered Audio—which offers a range of high-quality AUv3 plugins in the App Store, including the brilliant Battalion drum machine—had trouble bringing its Sinusoidal Run Rhythm to market. Michael Hetrick of Unfiltered Audio, who’s been in the iOS game for years, wrote on the Loopy Pro forum : Apple seems to be using AI for automated App Store reviews. SRR got rejected 4 times. The first time, they asked for a video of me demonstrating it (which almost always happens with our plugins). The second time, the editor hallucinated that “Polyharmonic” was an audio technology that we needed to show a documented license for to use the term in the description. The third time, it asked for a video again, this time with the app connected to the “required proprietary hardware”. The fourth time, it flagged SRR MIDI as spam because of its similarity to SRR. It was over a month of back-and-forth, so I threw my hands up and released it audio-only for now. What we will do is bundle the MIDI build into the binary so both AUv3s install. The app is now available, but only in the audio version. The MIDI version is still not out. AudioThing Materia took 25 days to get approved (1 rejection), and the latest Seconds , in collaboration with Hainbach, has been in review for 29 days and counting. The second case shows that this new Apple app review process AI reality can also cost app developers their livelihoods—especially those who have spent months coding their apps. The CRUX Synth Problem Marek Dendes is a new developer who is currently caught in this precarious situation. He has been working for several months on a flagship Synthesizer called CRUX Synth—a sort of “Serum 2” for iOS. I’ve been testing the beta for a few weeks now, and it truly is a flagship product. At the moment, it seems the synthesizer won’t be released, as the app has been rejected multiple times by Apple’s App Review process. He wrote in the Loopy Pro forum : My app was REJECTED from submission FOUR TIMES in row. Always same reason (eg. my app is “design spam” and “duplicates existing apps” and it is createed using “app generation template services”) as shown bellow in screenshots. Which is obvious nonsense. I replied on every rejection – no change, again rejected. Obviously nobody reads my explanations. Thing is it goes from “Waiting for Review” into “In Review” and then instantly in second to “Rejected” so this is some automated process and nobody even reads anything i write – so it’s a bit dead end. I submitted multiple appeals to the App Review Board – that did not help, did not get any reply (it’s about 5 days since first appeal submit). Tried also to submit only CRUX without effects to avoid multiple apps submitted at once – same result. There is nothing more i can do. I reached out to my contacts at Apple, but I didn’t get any real help from them regarding this case. My Two Cents (Opinion) iOS/iPadOS is a fantastic platform for making music on the go. It’s been part of my musical toolkit from the start, and for more than six years, it’s also played an integral role in my hybrid live performance setup. If you need to submit an app now for release before year’s end, that’s genuinely problematic: you could wait three weeks only to have it rejected. I’m in daily contact with iOS developers. Many have lost their former euphoria; instead, they express disillusionment and doubt that things will ever be the same. Developers are frustrated by lengthy release delays—and remember, not all submissions are music apps. With so many new apps launching, even great ones get lost. Do you remember what was published two days ago? This reflects a problem Apple created years ago: ending its affiliate program left media outlets unable to cover iOS meaningfully. That’s why I’m on Patreon. Today, written coverage of iOS music apps is rare unless they’re backed by major names like Roland, Korg, or Moog. The iOS market is currently off-kilter—not just because of the flood of AI apps, but also because of Apple itself. Where is the real Apple Intelligence when you actually need it? If they don’t get a handle on this and start reaching out to iOS developers in person again, as they did early on, I can see the market entering a strange period. Hey Claude, take me back to the App Store era of 2022. Right now! More information here: Apple iOS News supported by Patreon

title: Why is Google cutting off Search from AI-free schools? Here are some theories
abstract:
NPR > K-12 Education Why is Google cutting off Search from AI-free schools? Here are some theories By Sequoia Carrillo Friday, November 13, 2026 • 5:00 AM EST Catch up on what you missed with our Education newsletter, sent weekly. Google is a big part of the school day for millions of students. It's not only a search engine. It's a hub for sharing documents and turning in homework. An announcement this month makes it clear: Google wants AI to be a part of that education ecosystem. Many parents do not. "Parents are angry," said Jodi Carreon, a mom in Southern California. "They're very angry." Related Story: NPR When Carreon, who also runs the advocacy group Schools Beyond Screens , first read that Google was letting schools turn off AI features for students, she was excited. Her group is part of the parent-led movement demanding limits on technology in the classroom . But even as districts including Los Angeles Unified , Seattle Public Schools and New York City Public Schools recently agreed to bans on AI in the classroom, Google did not. If schools don't want AI Overviews to appear when students use its flagship Search tool, the company said, they will lose access to Google Search altogether. Even advocates who want less tech in schools know losing the ability to "Google" something will be an issue for teachers. In a post on X , New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani said Google is using "its monopoly power to force AI into our public schools," and Democratic Sen. Ed Markey of Massachusetts wrote to Google's CEO demanding the company reverse its policy. A baffling move Tracy Pizzo worked at Google for more than a decade before leaving the company in 2022. Much of her time at the company was focused on education and ethical AI standards. Google's move this month baffled her, especially coming at a time when young people's use of AI is under such scrutiny. She has a theory about why the tech giant is taking this stance: It could be linked to two recent court cases Google fended off in D.C. Google was sued by big online publishers who said adding AI overview to search negatively affected their business. The publishers sued under antitrust laws, and their argument hinged on convincing the court that AI Overviews was a separate product from Google Search. "The judge decided that Search and AI are an integrated product," Pizzo said, and subsequently dismissed the cases. "Now if Google were to provide an off switch for schools only … that's evidence that they can be separated. And that undermines the win they just had in court." When asked for comment, Google directed NPR to its original announcement , where the company said, "Our goal is simple: provide school leaders the control and confidence to use AI products in classrooms as they see fit." The company did not respond to additional questions by NPR about any connection between its announcement and recent antitrust cases. NPR asked antitrust experts about this theory. They weren't entirely convinced, but also didn't dismiss it altogether. The "AI or nothing" approach In any case, Google's AI Overviews doesn't get high marks from some watchdogs. Common Sense Media, a nonprofit that evaluates how teens interact with technology, recently gave the product an " unacceptable risk " rating. Among other things, Common Sense dinged the tool for unsafe content and citing false information. The day after the announcement, Google came under fire for another AI product in schools. Parents in North Carolina sued the company after Google's chatbot, Gemini, helped their 13-year-old daughter plan her suicide and funeral on her school-issued Chromebook. Even some of Google's longtime partners are surprised by the company's current position, including superintendent Hank Thiele in Illinois. Related Story: NPR "It may have caused a lot of damage in the trust that Google has built in education," he said. Thiele has worked with Google Classroom for almost two decades and says the company has always been a great partner. His district, made up entirely of high school students, is in the process of figuring out AI for its students. As an early adopter of tech in the classroom, he wants to be on top of it with AI. He said he thinks the company will listen to people's feedback but they bungled the messaging. "Google should have just plainly said, 'Our bad,'" Thiele said. "That would have been the appropriate response to a school." The "AI or nothing" approach, as Thiele put it, did not land well. Edited by Nirvi Shah and Nicole Cohen Google is a financial supporter of NPR.

title: Chicago schools to Google – we'd rather lose Search than be forced to accept AI
abstract:
Serving tech enthusiasts for over 25 years. TechSpot means tech analysis and advice you can trust . Ripple effect: Not long after Google announced its definitely-not-petulant response to schools banning its AI services by threatening to remove its search engine completely, Chicago Public Schools has said it will simply use a different search solution. Google's actions have also led to protests against the company, with demonstrators chanting the catchy slogan, "Hey Google, nice try. We don't want your Gemini." At the start of November, Chris Phillips, Google's vice president and general manager for education, said K-12 schools will soon have to accept the company's AI services to retain student access to its search engine. The reason, he claimed , was that Search and AI are now deeply integrated services. Instead of the usual results, students will see a message from their school stating that the services are not available. A lot of people didn't take this well, claiming Google was essentially blackmailing schools into using a service they didn't want. Chalkbeat Chicago reports that it led to protests in Cambridge, Massachusetts, and in Chicago, where the city's school district recently blocked student access to generative AI tools such as Gemini. Chicago Public Schools (CPS) has yet to respond to Google's announcement, but a CPS spokesperson said in a statement that the district was "actively exploring all options to independently suppress" the AI Overviews that appears at the top of Google searches. The spokesperson added that if CPS cannot provide students access to Google's search engine without its AI feature, the district will "look to other search solutions." It's not just CPS that's unhappy about Google's behavior. About 30 protesters, including parents, educators, and students, demonstrated outside Google's office in Chicago's West Loop. "We are owed lessons and feedback from the people CPS hired, people who are passionate and dedicated to making learning fun," said Reese Mackey, a junior at Kenwood Academy High School. "Not by a bot whose only job is to be a yes man and compile random sources from the internet for a nonsensical answer." A Google spokesperson said the company was working to improve Search for classroom use, including testing its "Guided Learning" feature, which uses AI to guide students through problems one step at a time instead of simply giving them answers. Chicago is far from alone in pushing back. In October, Frederick County's school board voted 6 – 1 to restrict student AI use from pre-K through 12th grade, just weeks after allowing older students to try Gemini with teacher permission. Board members raised concerns about the lack of warning to parents and teachers' inability to disable the tool on student devices. Exceptions remain for lessons about AI and accommodations for students with disabilities. New York City also introduced a one-year moratorium on student-facing generative AI from preschool through eighth grade for the 2026 – 2027 school year. High school use is limited to approved tools in supervised pilot or career-readiness programs, while Los Angeles has temporarily blocked generative AI tools on student devices across all grades. Google faces an uphill battle to convince schools that using AI is the way forward for students, but threatening to remove search from those who say no is hardly going to help convince them otherwise. 15 comments 3.4K likes and shares See more TechSpot in Google Add us as a preferred source and our reporting shows up first when you search. title: Show HN: Kapso – Iterative learning from enterprise data
abstract: Hey HN! We're Alireza and Majid building Leeroo ( https://leeroo.com/ ). Previously we’ve built AI systems for products with millions of users, including at LinkedIn and Meta. We’re now focusing on building AI systems for enterprise data. Today, we're open-sourcing Kapso ( https://github.com/Leeroo-AI/kapso ), an engine that runs experiments, deploys the best solution, and learns from every run. The nature of data work is iterative: investigate, form hypotheses, experiment, and improve based on what you learn. This bottom-up process is the only way to deliver meaningful outcomes quickly in large, messy enterprise data environments. Consultants gathering context in meetings or teams defining a business ontology upfront to fit into the data has no chance of execution, in quarters and sometimes years. An AI-native system should automate this process, compounding learning to each new investigation and implementation. For instance, one of our enterprise projects was moving a company off its old data estate onto a lakehouse with more than 30 source-system families, thousands of tables and transformations, and hundreds of BI reports. No individual or AI agent knew how that data estate was connected and operated. The only way to learn it was to investigate the company's repos, dbt models, documentation, and data itself and propose hypotheses about the estate, run experiments, and learn from them, until we understand how each system behaves and under which conditions. The iterative work goes beyond understanding how data and systems fit together, and the business operations. Building useful software is iterative too. Whether you’re optimizing a warehouse, building a lakehouse pipeline or predicting churn, you need to run experiments and learn what works best in that environment. As you deliver more projects, that know-how compounds, similar in principle to RL. RAGing documentation has little value until it has been tried in a specific environment and the consequences are learned. As with human engineering work, experimentation and learning should happen in a sandbox. We built Kapso for this kind of work, you give it an objective and success criteria, and it works towards an optimum solution that can be deployed on your stack. You can view a video walkthrough here:  https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=W4FHlza1fRs  Here’s how it works… Kapso has a bank of lessons that are induced or deduced from the past experiments, and each carries a credence score, conditions on where it applies, and the evidence behind it.  For each new experiment, an ideation module proposes ideas considering the earlier lessons, re-ranks them by expected return against the budget each would use, and sends the top-ranked ones to the implementor. Because the bank keeps learning from the past experiments in that environment, the proposed ideas are better suited to it than generic hypotheses from an LLM or RAG. Also, results of each experiment are verified by a verifier module that no experiment can access and cheat. As we’ve found when building such systems, sometimes the success criteria and evaluation tests need to be evolved. The experimentation modules can propose updates to the metrics and criteria for the verifier to approve or reject. After each run, learn() updates the bank of lessons’ scores and boundaries using the evidence from that run. Changes to the bank can also be A/B tested by running otherwise identical builds with the previous and updated banks. The bank is built on git, so you can share your experience with others, list the banks available to you, and update them (`kapso experience share/list/update` in CLI). The system is model-agnostic and coding-agent-agnostic. kapso.deploy(solution, target_stack) follows the same workflow, runs a shorter experimentation loop to adapt the best solution to the target stack (e.g. Docker, Modal, BentoCloud, LangGraph). Every domain has a harness to start from, you can write your own domain harness with /kapso:harness in the plugin or through CLI (kapso harness new <name>), and compound over that by running experimentations. We ran it on some public benchmarks and live competitions, with the following results… - Predictive modelling on relational databases: first on RelBench, Kumo AI (now Nvidia) and Stanford's benchmark, ahead of the best tabular foundation model ( https://star-project.stanford.edu/relbench/leaderboard/ ). This shows that keeping the learning in the harness-level can beat foundational table models. Updating a bank of lessons costs far less than retraining a tabular foundation model. - ML Engineering: First on OpenAI's MLE-bench at submission, still among the top open-source systems ( https://github.com/openai/mle-bench/pull/107 ). - AI competitions: ahead of the best agent the ALE-Bench authors at Sakana AI reported, and running autonomously at the live International Olympiad in AI 2026, above all 471 human contestants and in the top three AI systems ( https://ioai-official.org/ai-models-track/ioai%c2%b2-2026-re... ). We have a public bank for ML and Data at Leeroopedia ( https://leeroopedia.com/ ): around 100k pages extracted by experimenting on papers and repos, about 6M requests a month, about 28% from AI agents. If you are at a growing company with a complex data estate across multiple systems and functions, and your data and AI team is stretched, we would love to help!  https://github.com/Leeroo-AI/kapso

title: Show HN: Apron Chat Protocol
abstract: Hi HN friends - I've been obsessed with chat protocols for ages - one previous project is ssh-chat ( https://ssh.chat/ ) I come bringing a new kind of chat protocol that I've been working on since I spent quite a lot of time exploring the 14 other competing standards we've come up with in the past few decades. The protocol details are here:  https://apron.chat  I'm hoping that Apron will better reflect our needs beyond 2026, which I expect will move more and more toward semi-private chats rather than global social networks. Come say hi on the live public demo:  https://web.apron.chat  Some fun facts: - The demo server runs in a Cloudflare Durable Worker. It's quite efficient, since it's hibernated except for when a message comes in. Easy to self-host this in the free tier. - Despite the JSON protocol being intentionally unabbreviated ("message" instead of "msg", etc), a typical Apron session still uses almost half as much bandwidth and messages compared to an equivalent Matrix or XMTP session. This is largely because Apron minimizes the number of roundtrips and state required for common chat scenarios. Also it compresses very nicely! - The official reference client is a PWA (Apron Web), we also have a TUI, macOS, and an iOS implementation by third party Apron-enjoyers. There's two reference server implementations (Cloudflare worker in TS and a Go implementation), plus a bunch of minimal implementations. - My favourite fun capability is embedding streaming messages, great for LLM outputs. This can be done just by piping to a curl command, no additional dependencies. There's also a mode for streaming a terminal (by piping something like `script` from util-linux which handles row/col/baud flushing, no special dependencies either). See section 4.8 for details:  https://apron.chat/protocol#48-embeds-and-avatars

title: AWS Lambda Web Functions keep billing memory ~7 minutes after the last request
abstract:
Why we chose our own compute over Lambda Lambda Web Functions kept billing memory for 5–7 minutes after the last request, so we built our own compute. It answers warm requests 1.5–3× faster. Author Sean Whiteman Founder, Easel.sh Published Nov 11, 2026 Reading time 4 min Engineering We built our own compute. Then benchmarked it against AWS. When AWS announced Lambda Web Functions in October, I was excited. At Easel , we'd spent months building infrastructure to run web applications efficiently on traditional Lambda. Native HTTP servers, concurrent requests, and active CPU billing sounded like exactly what we'd been looking for. If Web Functions worked the way we hoped, we could potentially replace a substantial amount of our custom infrastructure. So we decided to put them to the test. A few weeks later, we'd decided to run our own compute instead. And as it turns out, our own infrastructure was faster, too. The five-minute problem Our initial experiments were promising. Web Functions handled 300 concurrent requests without errors, and a new function was serving requests in under nine seconds. But we quickly ran into something that didn't work for us. AWS documents that Web Functions bill for memory throughout an execution environment's lifetime, even when no requests are running. What the documentation doesn't specify is how long an idle environment will remain alive before being terminated. In our tests, environments continued running and accruing memory charges for 5–7 minutes after their last request. Across six representative environments, we measured idle periods of 313–411 seconds. There was no configurable idle timeout to shorten them. 5–7 min of memory billed after the last request Last request Idle, memory billed Lower is better 5 min 313s 355s 358s 391s 410s 411s 0 1m 2m 3m 4m 5m 6m 7m Six environments after their last completed request, us-east-1, October 26. For a 200ms request followed by 345 seconds of inactivity, that's roughly 1,700 times the request duration in metered memory time . We checked the economics against CloudWatch and AWS Cost Explorer. Across our experiment, memory accounted for approximately 88% of the calculated compute and request costs at published list prices, even though our application only used around 160–210 MB. The entire experiment amounted to about two cents at list prices. Hardly alarming on its own. For an application receiving steady traffic, this may not matter much. The same environment can serve many requests, spreading the idle-memory cost across them. But Easel needs to support thousands of applications with unpredictable traffic, including many that receive only a handful of requests per day. For those workloads, an environment might spend five minutes waiting for traffic after serving a request that took only a few milliseconds. Multiply that across thousands of independent deployments, and the economics start to look very different. We even tried terminating environments ourselves after 10 seconds of inactivity. That reduced metered environment time by roughly 20×, but AWS recorded every intentional exit as a runtime failure. It wasn't something we wanted to rely on in production. What if we ran the compute ourselves? Rather than adopt Web Functions, we decided to move application execution onto servers we operate ourselves, keeping traditional Lambda available for overflow. This gives us control over scheduling and resource allocation. We can share capacity across applications without paying AWS for each idle environment, and scale beyond our own infrastructure when demand requires it. Easel.sh edge Easel.sh compute Lambda overflow Serving Idle Requests enter the Easel.sh edge, which routes them to our own compute, where many apps share one machine. Lambda takes only the overflow. Our first self-operated compute host went live in US East on November 2, serving applications including Easel's own website. But taking ownership of the compute raised another question: How would our performance compare to AWS? We deployed the same Next.js 16 application to both platforms and ran a series of benchmarks from a client in Ashburn, Virginia. The results surprised us. 1.5–3× faster warm requests on the same Next.js app Easel.sh AWS Lambda Web Functions Median ms · lower is better JSON API 2.9 × 9.3 27.0 Server-side rendering 2.1 × 12.2 26.0 Streaming (first chunk) 2.0 × 9.1 18.1 CPU-intensive API 1.5 × 39.7 61.4 Median time to first byte (first chunk for streaming), excluding the TLS handshake. 100 requests per route per platform from Ashburn, Virginia. Our host delivered 1.5–3× faster median warm-request times across all four workloads. The difference wasn't limited to network or routing overhead. Running the same 20,000 chained SHA-256 operations took 29.2ms on our host versus 43.8ms on Web Functions, about 1.5× faster. And cold starts told a similar story. After leaving both applications idle for 12 minutes, we triggered fresh execution environments on each platform. 3.5× faster cold starts after 12 minutes idle Fastest to slowest of two trials Lower is better Easel.sh : 216 – 250 ms AWS Lambda Web Functions : 810 – 854 ms First request after 12 minutes idle, sent to both platforms at the same moment. Time to first byte, excluding the TLS handshake. Two paired trials only. In both trials, Easel started serving requests about 3.5× faster . We also saw an interesting difference after a shorter idle period. Following one five-minute gap, Web Functions had already terminated its environment and needed 908ms to respond. Easel resumed its paused environment and responded in just 14ms. These are early results from a single region and a small application, not a comprehensive performance study. The cold-start comparison has only two paired samples, and we haven't benchmarked sustained throughput yet. Still, seeing our own infrastructure outperform AWS across these initial workloads was encouraging. Taking ownership of the infrastructure Running our own compute comes with additional responsibilities. We have to manage capacity, handle failures, and make sure resources are distributed efficiently across applications. But it also gives us the freedom to optimize the entire execution path, rather than working around the constraints of another platform. Web Functions may be a good fit for applications with sustained traffic, where idle memory costs are less significant. For Easel, the economics of running large numbers of independent applications led us in a different direction. And our initial benchmarks suggest that the decision doesn't have to come at the expense of performance. We're taking on more infrastructure complexity so developers using Easel don't have to. How we measured Dates Benchmarks ran November 11–12, 2026 (UTC). Idle-memory measurements are from October 26, 2026. Setup The same Next.js 16 application on Easel's self-operated US East host and on AWS Lambda Web Functions in us-east-1. Client One client in Ashburn, Virginia. Timing Time to first byte, excluding TLS connection setup but including network transit and platform routing. Samples About 100 requests per route per platform for warm requests. Two paired trials for cold starts. Hardware The platforms ran on different hardware and resource configurations, so these compare deployments, not normalized hardware. Pricing AWS costs use published list prices. Sources AWS Lambda Web Functions Web Functions environment lifecycle Web Functions scaling behavior AWS Lambda pricing

title: Nintendo Takes Down Emulators and Firmware in Massive GitHub DMCA Sweep
abstract:
Nintendo has sent four DMCA takedown notices to GitHub targeting two Nintendo Switch emulators, Yuzu and Citron Neo, along with mod chip firmware. This isn't the first time Nintendo has sent takedown notices to GitHub, and it's not even the first time it's tried to take down Yuzu , but the focus this time around seems to be on firmware for mod chips. This particular firmware had 144 repositories, all of which have been removed by GitHub and replaced by a DMCA takedown notice. Mod chips like Picofly can be soldered onto the Nintendo Switch's mainboard, and can be flashed with this firmware to circumvent Nintendo's copy protection. GitHub has posted Nintendo's November 6 DMCA notice , which says, "The Nintendo Switch console and video games contain technological protection measures ('TPMs') that permit the Nintendo Switch console to interact only with legitimate Nintendo video game files. This process protects Nintendo’s copyright-protected video games, (...) by preventing users from playing pirated copies of Nintendo’s video games on the Nintendo Switch console and by preventing users from unlawfully copying and playing Nintendo’s video games on unauthorized devices." A History of Every Nintendo Direct in the Switch Era and Beyond View 27 Images However, while this takedown has effectively wiped out a ton of repositories with mod chip firmware, it seems like it's still being hosted elsewhere on the site, according to TorrentFreak . It's possible, though, that Nintendo isn't finished yet; back in 2024, Nintendo effectively took down 8,500 copies of Yuzu by issuing a takedown that targeted 12 different mirrors of the emulator. This particular takedown also comes a few days after emulators were able to run the remake of The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time on PC, so this could be a sign that Nintendo is winding up its lawyers to crack down on emulation once again. If anything, emulation is a completely different beast in 2026 than it was even in 2024, thanks to the rise of AI. There's already been a wave of AI-made mashup mods that took over Twitter for a couple of weeks, and led Anthropic to coding in a lock to prevent Claude from outright copying games . Game developers have started cracking down on AI ports of games, too. Just last month Rockstar had to take down a browser version of GTA 5 , and Bethesda took down an AI-generated Fallout New York game . Jacqueline Thomas Senior Tech Editor Jackie Thomas is the Senior Tech Editor at IGN and the PC components queen. She's been covering gaming hardware for more than a decade for IGN, TechRadar, Gizmodo, PC Gamer and more. You can follow her @Jackiecobra 0 88

No results found View all tags ortuman released this 13 Nov 14:22 v0.3.0 784ad60 This commit was created on GitHub.com and signed with GitHub’s verified signature . GPG key ID: B5690EEEBB952194 Verified Learn about vigilant mode . The big one in this release is federation: Lonewolf can now talk to other XMPP servers. We also added direct TLS and a handful of extensions that desktop clients rely on. Lonewolf is still pre-1.0 and runs as a single node. Full XMPP compliance and clustering are on the roadmap . What's new Federation Your users can now exchange messages, presence, IQs, and roster subscriptions with people on other XMPP servers. If a host has a certificate and a public DNS name, federation is on by default, with nothing extra to configure. Lonewolf authenticates peers by certificate only. The other server needs a trusted certificate and SASL EXTERNAL support. We don't support Server Dialback. When the other server supports it, both directions share a single connection ( XEP-0288 ). Servers also tell each other their stanza size and idle limits up front ( XEP-0478 ). Federation checks certificate revocation lists published by the CA, fetched over plain HTTP. If a CRL can't be downloaded, the connection goes ahead anyway. You can turn downloads off with s2s.tls.fetch_crls = false , or point s2s.tls.crls_path at a local file to use only that. Direct TLS Clients and servers can now connect with TLS from the first byte ( XEP-0368 ), using new dedicated listeners. Outbound federation discovers both STARTTLS and direct TLS endpoints. More for desktop clients Private XML Storage ( XEP-0049 ) gives clients a place to keep private settings and legacy bookmarks. Software Version ( XEP-0092 ) answers "what server is this?" queries. It doesn't reveal the operating system unless you turn that on. Both are enabled by default. Short-lived certificates Use letsencrypt.certificate_profile to pick one of the profiles your CA advertises, including short-lived certificates. If you change the profile, Lonewolf renews early so the new one takes effect right away. SCRAM-SHA-512 (opt-in) You can now enable SCRAM-SHA-512 and SCRAM-SHA-512-PLUS. Be aware that they come from an expired Internet-Draft , not an RFC, and aren't registered with IANA. Even if you leave SHA-512 login disabled, new accounts and password changes now store credentials that v0.2.0 can't read, so rolling back isn't straightforward. See the standards reference for exactly what's supported and the configuration reference for every setting and its default. Build from source Grab Source code (tar.gz) or Source code (zip) below, extract it, and run: cargo build --release --locked -p lonewolf -p lonewolfctl -p lonewolfbench The benchmark tool is now called lonewolfbench instead of lonewolf-bench , so update any scripts that call it. All you need is a stable Rust toolchain and a system linker on Linux or macOS. The quick start walks you through setup. Full changelog: v0.2.0…v0.3.0 Licensed under Apache-2.0 . title: NYC Council passes ban on 'surveillance pricing'
abstract:
The City Council passed a bill Thursday that bans companies in New York City from using surveillance pricing, which charges different prices based on algorithms or shoppers’ personal data. Surveillance pricing means shoppers see a price based on their personal data like demographics, credit, browsing history or purchasing history. The bill prohibits surveillance pricing both online and in stores, although the practice is mainly used on the web. Speaker Julie Menin described surveillance pricing as an “insidious and predatory corporate practice” that erodes privacy and fairness. “It's a practice that worsens the affordability crisis, and today it's a practice that we are going to be ending,” she said during a press conference ahead of the vote. In one investigation cited by the Council, Target shoppers saw a jump in pricing based on location data showing whether they were inside or outside a store. Shoppers found that a 55-inch SmartTV cost $499 on the Target app when inside a store, and $599 when in the store parking lot. Uber, Lyft, Target, Instacart and airlines are among the companies that have faced scrutiny for alleged surveillance pricing. Many of the companies have denied using the practice. Under the bill, the city would be able to issue fines of up to $1,000 for each transaction that violates the ban. Menin’s proposal follows legislation approved by Albany lawmakers in June that prohibits surveillance pricing online and in stores, with some exceptions. Mayor Zohran Mamdani said in a statement that he supports the ban. He called surveillance pricing “just another way corporations are finding to squeeze working people.” “New Yorkers’ personal data should never be used as a weapon against their own pocketbooks,” he added. Business groups have warned that the ban could hinder discounts or loyalty programs for customers. “If enacted, this law will make it harder for small restaurants with limited marketing budgets to reach customers, putting them at a disadvantage against national chains,” said Josh Gold, a spokesperson for Uber. The company operates Uber Eats, which allows restaurants to offer discounts based on search history and previous orders. Menin said the legislation would not affect discounts.

title: Jensen Huang Admitted He Was Facing an "Avalanche" of Excess Wafers and Memory
abstract:
Before Resigning, Jensen Huang Admitted He Was Facing an “Avalanche” of Excess Wafers and Memory, New Report Sheds More Light on the GPU & RAM Crisis Sikandar Mahmood November 13, 2026 Support us for free For the past two years, the narrative around inflated GPU and RAM prices has been the insatiable AI demand eating up wafer at TSMC and every module on Earth must go to AI data centers. However, the narrative is cracking ever since reports of channel stuffing and over commitments came out. Now with Nvidia’s former CEO Jensen Huang gone, more details are out that corroborate our earlier reports on inflated demand on AI. According to Wall Street Journal , Huang admitted in August that major cloud providers are moving away from Nvidia in favor of in-house chips, leaving Nvidia staring down a massive oversupply of prepaid TSMC silicon and memory that was “coming at him like an ‘avalanche'”. The WSJ report details a heated clash in August 2026 between Huang and Nvidia’s longtime Chief Financial Officer, Colette Kress, the executive who has now taken over as Nvidia’s interim CEO. Kress was concerned about Nvidia’s growing financial exposure and wanted to rein in the company’s “circular financing” commitments to cloud providers, and AI companies like OpenAI and Anthropic. While early talks had floated backstopping roughly 8 gigawatts of OpenAI compute (worth up to $250 billion), Kress successfully scaled Nvidia’s signed guarantee cap down to roughly 4.25 gigawatts, or up to $125 billion. In an August meeting, Huang belittled Kress for questioning the deals, calling her “a deer in the headlights”. To justify why Nvidia needed to financially backstop OpenAI and smaller cloud providers to keep buying its GPUs, Huang admitted that Nvidia was caught in a massive squeeze. Then he went on to describe the situation the company was in. Major cloud providers were running away from Nvidia, making plans to use alternative chips and lessen their reliance on the firm. Even worse, Huang said, the vast supply of chip wafers and memory Nvidia had committed to buying were coming at him like an ‘avalanche.’ Per the WSJ Nvidia has reportedly contacted TSMC to wind down their chip orders. For PC builders and hardware enthusiast the reported admission is validating, and quite glaring. title: Brave Search API now accepts agentic payments via the x402 protocol
abstract:
The Brave Search API , our developer tool for building applications with data from the Web, is adding support for instant, pay-as-you-go, agentic payments enabled by the open x402 payment protocol. Developers and autonomous AI agents that specifically require agentic search can now programmatically query Brave’s independent search index, ground agent responses, and settle requests in real time, which eliminates the need for traditional API key management. Integrating x402 with the Brave Search API makes it easier for an agentic harness to leverage Brave Search API via a CLI wallet, as Brave runs its own facilitator accepting USDC on the Base blockchain, with acceptance on other networks and with other stablecoins incoming soon. This allows a Brave Search API user the ability to pay for LLM Context (agentic grounding) or general web search on-demand, without first creating an account and selecting a plan. Instead, simply transfer USDC stablecoin to your agent’s wallet via the Base network and it’s ready to access the same high-quality search results powered by Brave’s search engine. How does it work? Brave Search API endpoints behind x402 require payment on every request rather than authentication. A request sent without payment receives an HTTP 402 Payment Required response that states the price of that search and the payment details needed to pay it. The agent signs a USDC payment for that amount and retries the request with the signed payment attached. Once the payment is verified, the search runs and results are returned with a receipt of the transaction that occurred on the Base blockchain. Get started today Pricing follows Brave’s published API rates: LLM Context, an API designed specifically for providing search context for agents, will cost $0.005 ($5 per 1,000). Additionally, web (search for humans), news, image, video, and local endpoints will also be available for $0.005 ($5 per 1,000). Gas fees for transacting on the Base blockchain will be covered for a limited time. Since each request carries its own payment, a Brave Search API account is no longer needed to use the service. The easiest path to query via x402 is to install Purl Wallet, a Stripe-developed CLI wallet for your agent. Set up your wallet, top it off using Base-native USDC, and start querying today. Ready to build pay-as-you-go search into your apps or AI agents? Check out our Brave Search x402 Proxy Documentation and explore: https://api-dashboard.search.brave.com/documentation/guides/agent-payments

Selecting Orchestrator (Carbon) from the model selector in Google Antigravity. In just a couple of days, tens of thousands of swarms have been launched on Antigravity, pushing frontier intelligence on the hardest problems. For everyday feature work and debugging inside a single session, running a frontier reasoning model with multiple parallel agents on every step of every routine task slows down your loop and burns frontier quota. A common industry approach is to use a static “model router” that guesses task difficulty from your first prompt and routes the entire task to the cheapest model that is good enough to complete the task. Unfortunately, these start breaking down as agents become longer running, requiring different levels of complexity at different stages, often discovered as the task evolves. Orchestrator takes a dynamic, bidirectional approach between Carbon and Gemini 4 Hydrogen within the evolution of a single trajectory. For example, Carbon can start in a read-only phase to explore dependencies, resolve ambiguities, and build a concrete plan with explicit re-planning triggers. Hydrogen could then take over to write edits, update packages, and run tests. If Hydrogen hits friction, it would hand back to Carbon to inspect the state, repair the plan, and resume execution. This allows Orchestrator to reach near-Carbon task success while being faster and more quota-efficient. On Terminal-Bench 4.1, Orchestrator reached near-Carbon task success rates while, on average, consuming 24% less quota and completing 19% faster. title: Use and perceptions of AI tools among Australian general practice registrars: a national survey.
abstract:
INTRODUCTION
Artificial intelligence (AI) tools are increasingly used in health care, yet little is known about how often Australian general practitioner trainees (GP registrars) use them or how they perceive the impact of AI on training and clinical care.


AIM
This study aimed to examine how frequently registrars use AI tools for clinical care and education, types of AI used, the perceived benefits and risks, and training needs.


METHODS
A national cross-sectional online survey conducted from 7 May to 4 June 2024 invited 3743 Australian General Practice Training or Fellowship Support Program registrars to participate. The survey assessed frequency and context of AI use, practice-level adoption, perceived impacts, training exposure, and ethical-legal concerns. Analyses were descriptive.


RESULTS
Among the 727 respondents (19.5%), frequent use (weekly or more) was uncommon; 7.3% for clinical tasks, 5.0% for education. Practice-level adoption was low, with 10.8% reporting subscription to AI tools. Most registrars anticipated benefits, particularly learning efficiency and administrative workload reduction. However, 25.0% perceived increased medicolegal risk. Formal training was rare, with most relying on self-directed learning, though many rated AI education as important. Among clinical users, common tools included large language models (32.5%), remote patient monitoring devices (28.6%), and voice-to-text tools (26.2%). Large language models predominated in education (63.5%).


DISCUSSION
In May-June 2024, AI tool use among registrars was limited, although most perceived potential benefit. Enthusiasm was tempered by concerns about safety, ethics, and legal risks. Structured training and guidelines are needed to support safe, effective integration into GP registrars' practice and education.
